Date: Tue, 26 Mar 2013 08:03:12 -0500
To: heather.r.white@usdoj.gov
Cc: "Harper, Karen" <karen.harper@covidien.com>,
    "Tetzlaff, Gail S" <gail.tetzlaff@covidien.com>,
    "Spaulding, Eileen L." <eileen.spaulding@covidien.com>


Dear Ms. White,



Attached are orders Mallinckrodt has received within the last business day that we are reporting to the Drug Enforcement Administration as suspicious orders pursuant to 21 CFR 1301.74(b).  These orders are on hold and will not be shipped unless, and until, Mallinckrodt's Controlled Substances Compliance Group completes its independent analysis of these suspicious orders and determines that the orders are not likely to be diverted into other than legitimate medical, scientific and industrial channels.



If you have any questions or concerns regarding this report, please contact Don Lohman at 314-654-3927.



Best regards,

Subject:        2011 Procurement forecasts

Dave,

I mentioned this in conversation last week, but wanted to get it written down.

As far as I know, the basic premis for JDA is the same as BPCS.  For demand out several years, ending inventory defaults to minimum + 1 run.  For example, Oxycodone 886599 minimum is 1200 Kg. and 887399 is 700 Kg.  Inventory is added in 1500 Kg increments, so forecasted inventory will be between 1900 and 4900 Kg (with both items forecasting below minimum) with all the intermediates defaulting to zero.  In fact oxycodone inventory runs much higher and this is one of the products with intermediates on hand 12/31.

How do I get target inventories for December 31, 2011? 
Should I ignore JDA and get the numbers by hand from planning?
Should I assume constant inventories?

I do think we need to forecast demand better than plus or minus 3,000 kg.

To: Harper, Karen; Mannino, Tony; Ratliff, Bill; Hunter, Dave; Pokorny, Camille M
Subject: RE: Request Advice on Customer Order for Material to Prepare Reference Standard
Karen,

Last year (2008) I dispensed 63.5 grams of Codeine Phosphate reference standard for the analytical support of our
manufacturing of the bulk here in St. Louis and all the dosage forms in Hobart. So far this year (2009) I have dispensed 13


   grams. Last year Sherryl Ruder shipped one order for 200 milligrams to an external customer and had no internal requests for
Codeine Phosphate.

If I were to subdivide 1000 grams, that would last us almost 16 years at the rate that we used it in 2008. I must say that our
reference standard use is increasing, so that 1000 grams may only last maybe 10 years. That still is a very long time to store a
qualified reference. I also know that storing any controlled substance that long invites opportunities for diversion. So that
generally should be discouraged.

We use the manufacturing registration for our operation. When it is shipped to Hobart  it goes out under our manufacturing
registration and is transferred to Hobart's Analytical registration via their form 222.

It seems to me that if the customer is "manufacturing" a reference standard, it should be received into their manufacturing
registration. When it goes to their client to be used in the lab, that is when it should be transferred to analytical lab registration.

Ted
From: Harper, Karen
Sent: Friday, May 15, 2009 8:07 AM
To: Myrick, Ted
Cc: Pokorny, Camille M; Ratliff, Bill; Hunter, Dave
Subject: Request Advice on Customer Order for Material to Prepare Reference Standard
Ted
Controlled Substance Compliance and Security are working with Customer Service to determine the validity of a customer order
for 1 kg of Codeine Phosphate, within the scope of our Suspicious Order Monitoring Program.
Customer states their intended use is to "prepare a reference standard for a client who will use the material for testing activities".

Our concerns are:
The 1 kg quantity seems too large, does this exceed the quantity of API we would normally use internally to prepare reference
standards?
Does the intended use differ from the activity that you and Sherryl perform? Within Mallinckrodt, we use DEA Manufacturing
registration for the work you do in "making" ARS compounds, customer is requesting the material on an Analytical Lab DEA
registration.
Our regulatory interpretation is that use of Analytical Lab DEA registration is reserved for an entity that actually performs tests
on the material (example:
Gateway Medical Research obtains material on Analytical Lab DEA registration to perform clinical trial work)

Please comment and thank you.

Karen Harper

Feds raid a pair of pain clinics in city

By KATE HOWARD
Publication: Florida Times-Union (Jacksonville)
Date: {LexisNexis: 20100730}Friday, July 30 2010





{ID_Web_horizontal_sml_white}{ID_Web_horizontal_sml_white}



You are viewing page 1
 




Nearly all of the patients at a North Jacksonville pain clinic raided Thursday were prescribed the same remedy: the highly addictive pain killer oxycodone, the anti-anxiety medicine Xanax and a muscle relaxer called Soma. And the unassuming clinic, tucked away in a West 48th Street strip mall, did a staggering business.

Florida Department of Health records show that 611,000 oxycodone pills were dispensed by Duval Wellness Center in April and May alone.

The clinic and its owner, 78-year-old osteopathic physician Donald W. Hall, were issued a cease and desist order Wednesday by the health department.

About 10 a.m. Thursday, FBI and DEA agents and Jacksonville police burst into the clinic and First Coast Pain and Urgent Care on Normandy Boulevard, also owned by Hall.

No charges have been brought and no arrests were made in the months-old investigation, federal officials said.

The targeted businesses are among a growing number of pain management clinics registered in Jacksonville - with the number jumping from less than 50 in March to about 60 today.

"Pill mills" have been largely viewed as a South Florida problem. But as crackdowns and moratoriums on the pain clinics grew more intense in Broward County and nearby towns, many clinic owners opened shop farther north.

Steve Cole, spokesman for the U.S. Attorney's Office, said the Jacksonville investigation focused on the two clinics.

"We've had similar investigations like this throughout the Middle District of Florida, looking into pain clinics that may be dispensing prescription drugs illegally," he said. "Florida has had a problem with that. So we obviously are looking in all the major cities to see if and where there are problems."

FBI spokesman Jeff Westcott said he couldn't reveal any details about the investigation or the dozen search warrants executed Thursday.

About 99 percent of the 8,000 prescriptions issued by Duval Wellness in April and May were identical: oxycodone, Xanax and Soma, according to the health department. The state inspected the facility's medical records in early June and also found that they had been operating as a pain clinic without state authorization.

Hall, who has been practicing medicine for 40 years, couldn't be reached for comment.

A neighbor of Hall's, Pat Collins, said she saw lots of police activity at Hall's Lake City home early Thursday.

"He lives down the street and the police have been at his house all morning," Collins said.

Hall was disciplined by the state medical board once, in 1985, for dispensing dextroamphetamines for weight loss even though it wasn't approved for that use. He was reprimanded and ordered to pay a $1,000 fine.

Duval Wellness, at North Main and West 48th, opened in March but quickly became a mecca for out-of-state people seeking pain pills. Times-Union reporters who visited the location multiple times since April saw dozens of cars from Tennessee, Kentucky, Ohio and other states routinely lining the parking lot. Armed security guards patrolled the entrance to the clinic.

Children and parents crossed paths with the customers on a daily basis. A day care is located across the plaza from the clinic, and North Shore Elementary School is a short walk away.

At First Coast Pain and Urgent Care, the strip center parking lot was also filled with out-of-state plates, with people often waiting in their cars with the windows down until they were called in for their appointment.

As DEA agents carried out boxes filled with files Thursday, a man who identified himself as a patient walked up with his 2 p.m. appointment card to see what was going on.

He refused to give his name but said he thought the clinic with the blacked-out windows was on the up-and-up. He said he was a patient at S&P Medical in 2007, when the Jacksonville clinic was closed for illegally prescribing narcotics to patients without medical need.

He said he thought those doctors were over-prescribing but that the doctors at First Coast Pain required all his medical records and counseled him about the addictive nature of Roxicodone, the fast-acting pain killer he was prescribed.

"It looked to me like they were running legit," he said.

First Coast Pain has not been issued a closure order from the state, and Department of Health officials present during the raid Thursday were only gathering information, the agency said.

Records show that First Coast Pain is registered with the state as a pain clinic.

Times-Union writer Bridget Murphy contributed to this report.

Press Release
 
 
  MCKESSON AGREES TO PAY RECORD $150 MILLION SETTLEMENT FOR FAILURE TO REPORT SUSPICIOUS ORDERS OF PHARMACEUTICAL DRUGS
 
JAN 17 - (Washington, DC) – McKesson Corporation (McKesson), one of the nation’s largest distributors of pharmaceutical drugs, agreed to pay a record $150 million civil penalty for alleged violations of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA), the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) announced today.
 
The nationwide settlement requires McKesson to suspend sales of controlled substances from distribution centers in Colorado, Ohio, Michigan and Florida for multiple years. The staged suspensions are among the most severe sanctions ever agreed to by a DEA-registered distributor. The settlement also imposes new and enhanced compliance obligations on McKesson’s distribution system.
 
In 2008, McKesson agreed to a $13.25 million civil penalty and administrative agreement for similar violations. In this case, the government alleged again that McKesson failed to design and implement an effective system to detect and report “suspicious orders” for controlled substances distributed to its independent and small chain pharmacy customers– i.e. orders that are unusual in their frequency, size, or other patterns. From 2008 until 2013, McKesson supplied various U.S. pharmacies an increasing amount of oxycodone and hydrocodone pills, frequently misused products that are part of the current opioid epidemic.
 
The government’s investigation developed evidence that even after designing a compliance program after the 2008 settlement, McKesson did not fully implement or adhere to its own program. In Colorado, for example, McKesson processed more than 1.6 million orders for controlled substances from June 2008 through May 2013, but reported just 16 orders as suspicious, all connected to one instance related to a recently terminated customer. 
 
"This groundbreaking resolution is tough and appropriate and underscores our commitment to hold accountable all DEA registrants, including those who distribute controlled substances," said DEA Acting Administrator Chuck Rosenberg.  "DEA is committed to fighting the opioid epidemic with all of the tools at our disposal."
 
In addition to the monetary penalties and suspensions, the government and McKesson agreed to enhanced compliance terms for the next five years. Among other things, McKesson has agreed to specific, rigorous staffing and organizational improvements; periodic auditing; and stipulated financial penalties for failing to adhere to the compliance terms. Critically, the settlement will require McKesson to engage an independent monitor to assess compliance – the first independent monitor of its kind in a CSA civil penalty settlement.
 
This was a multi-district investigation that involved the following DEA Field Divisions:  Boston Field Division, Chicago Field Division, Denver Field Division, Detroit Field Division, Miami Field Division, New Jersey Field Division, San Francisco Field Division, St. Louis Field Division, and Washington Division Office. The following U.S. Attorneys’ Offices participated in the case: Central District of California, Eastern District of California, District of Colorado, Middle District of Florida, Eastern District of Kentucky, Northern District of Illinois, District of Massachusetts, Eastern District of Michigan, District of Nebraska, District of New Jersey, Northern District of West Virginia, and Western District of Wisconsin.
 
U.S. Attorneys’ Offices for the District of Colorado and the Northern District of West Virginia, along with DEA’s Office of Chief Counsel and its Diversion Control Division, led the civil settlement negotiations.  DEA’s Denver, Detroit and Miami Field Divisions and its Washington Division Office led the administrative and civil investigation. The U.S. Department of Justice Criminal Division’s Narcotic and Dangerous Drug Section (NDDS) also coordinated and assisted in negotiating certain portions of the settlement. Assistant United States Attorneys Amanda Rocque (Colorado) and Alan McGonigal (NDWV) represented the United States in the civil penalty investigations and negotiations.  Associate Chief Counsel Lee Reeves and Senior Attorneys Dedra Curteman, Dana Hill and Krista Tongring represented DEA in the investigations and negotiations. Trial Attorneys Harry Matz and Kirtland Marsh were involved for NDDS.

Kathy,

Just thought I should let you know that Keysource Medical has had their DEA license revoked as of June 10. See the news
release below from the DEA.

News Release [printer-friendly version]
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
June 10, 2011
Contact: Rich Isaacson
Number: (313) 234-4310
Cincinnati Pharmaceutical Supplier's DEA License Suspended
Keysource Medical distributed 48 million doses of oxycodone products to Florida pharm acies
JUN 10 - DETROIT- Robert L. Corso, Special Agent in Charge of the Detroit Field Division, Drug  Enforcement Administration
(DEA) announced today the immediate suspension of the federal controlled substance Registration of Keysource Medical, a
wholesale supplier of pharmaceuticals.
Keysource Medical, based in Cincinnati, Ohio, has been the subject of a DEA investigation that alleges the company was selling
large quantities of controlled substances to pharmacies, primarily in Florida. The investigation has revealed that several of
Keysource Medical's largest purchasers of oxycodone were engaged in schemes to dispense controlled substances based on
prescriptions that were written for other than legitimate medical purposes. The investigation revealed that Keystone Medical
distributed approximately 48 million dosage units of oxycodone products to customers in Florida over a two year time between
November of 2008 and November of 2010.
 Pharmaceutical companies have a responsibility to ensure that the drugs they sell don't end up in the hands of drug traffickers or
businesses that are conducting their business illegally,  said Corso.  Prescription drug abuse in Florida, southern Ohio and
northern Kentucky has risen to epidemic proportions, and Keysource Medical, should have known based on the large, frequent
quantities, that their customers were diverting oxycodone into arenas that were not legitimate. This action is another reminder
that the DEA is working hard to hold accountable those companies who choose to operate outside the law.
DEA's action suspends Keysource Medical's DEA Certificate of Registration in accordance with an Immediate Suspension Order
and pursuant to Sections 303 and 304 of the Controlled Substances Act, Title 21, Sections 823 and 824. The DEA's investigation
of Keysource Medical has determined that the continued registration of this company constitutes an imminent danger to public
health and safety.
Keysource Medical received written notice of the factual and legal basis for this action. In addition, Keysource Medical will be
given an opportunity for an administrative hearing within the next 60 days. After the  hearing, the DEA Deputy Administrator will


   make a final decision on whether Keysource Medical's registration should be permanently revoked. This decision will be
published in the Federal Register.
Oxycodone is the generic name of an addictive prescription painkiller that is classified under federal narcotics laws as a Schedule
II controlled substance. Oxycodone is typically legally prescribed to combat acute, severe pain for legitimate medical purposes.

INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.



 


EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 


EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.


 


EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.


 


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


 


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


 


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


 


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


 


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


 


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


 


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.


See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information<http://whatcounts.jobson.com/t?r=12&c=0&l=2982&ctl=54A39:B5F526631F6058485DD7F585132E82E093B8F18DA1535B1F&> and Medication Guide<http://whatcounts.jobson.com/t?r=12&c=0&l=2982&ctl=54A3A:B5F526631F6058485DD7F585132E82E093B8F18DA1535B1F&>.

Suspicious Order Monitoring
Cardinal Health's Suspicious Order Monitoring (SOM) program marries high-tech with high-touch to monitor all controlled substance orders placed by our customers
Three main components:
[*]   The "Know Your Customer" program
Our Know Your Customer program starts with a questionnaire that gives us a baseline assessment, including customer order history and public database verification. It continues with the on-going involvement of our sales force. Through routine customer site visits and periodic highlight reports to track customer-specific growth relative to industry growth, our Cardinal Health employees are well-positioned to notice any "red flags" of potential diversion and respond accordingly.
[*]   Electronic order monitoring
Electronic order monitoring is an enhanced "first-step" system that monitors controlled substance orders before they ever go through to a distribution center for fulfillment. Under this program, customers are assigned a monthly threshold for each family of controlled substances. If an order is placed that exceeds the threshold, that order is flagged and held for review by our Quality and Regulatory Affairs (QRA) department.
[*]   Investigation
Our monitoring program also includes an investigation component.  When circumstances warrant Cardinal Health sends trained investigators to visit pharmacy customers to gather information about the customer's handling of controlled substances.

                +31,000 Randi’s Scene Setter

David

 

From: Decker, John F
Sent: Monday, January 09, 2017 5:40 PM
To: Anderson, David <David.Anderson@mallinckrodt.com>; Hoke, Molly <Molly.Hoke@mallinckrodt.com>
Cc: Shah, Chirag <Chirag.Shah@mallinckrodt.com>
Subject: URGENT- finalize 2017 Sci Comm budgets
Importance: High



 

Team,

 

Please prioritize the action items in this memo. 

 

I realize, as well as any of you, how frustrating and time consuming the current budget discussions are.  I ask you to consider all this growing pains for MNK- this is all new to me; and, one way or another, that this current round will be resolved very soon (and we can all go back to Scientific Communications).  Our total budget, of $1.9 million, is based on what we spent last year.  I still maintain- there will be money for great ideas.  Don’t despair! 

 

I had a good discussion with Tunde around budgets for 2017.  He started the meeting by mentioning that he needs to save $9 million.  I know he is sincerely trying to do this without touching headcount- meaning, anything incremental to the $150 k/ brand we started with will only occur, if at all, after a debate.  He also said, what is not committed by July will be taken away.  (Interpret that as June, FYI- I’ve seen all this before).  Our ‘favorability’ in 2016 is a main source of these challenges.

 

In general:

·         We will prioritize projects that are ‘truly medical’, notable Medical Writing Grants (and Scientific Platform… And Review Articles… etc)

·         We will start to discuss, and build the case, that budgets for Company Sponsored Studies should come from R&D.  I will discuss Publication budgets for clinical trials, starting with Lawrence; I’m sure this discussion will get elevated to Steve’s level.  This will take some time; but it is now time to formalize this discussion. 

 

We can discuss the details, but here’s the bottom line:   I need to provide Christine and Tunde with a revised version of the attached, getting all brands down to $150K. David and Molly, a few specific action-item requests for you.  Chirag, you lucked out this time- but please note, we were $200K favorable for the Stub period- and that was mostly for ARD.  

 

Acthar: no action needed

 

Intrathecal: Max $150K.  David, please identify all committed spends here.  Tunde was very focused on IT during our meeting.  Knowing the IT Hydromorphone CSRs are due late in 2017…  but see above- is any of this ‘truly medical’?  We need to tease (at least identify) out what’s R&D… Needs to be discussed with Lawrence Hill

 

Ofirmev: Max $150K. 

·         David: We need to shift the ad board to Medical Affairs as discussed

·         ID budgets for R&D (PREA, UV Burn) and set aside as separate group Needs to be discussed with Lawrence Hill

·         Same with proposed Review Articles (2 for Randi in particular)

·         From this foundation, prioritize what we need to do but not yet budgeted- and then, how much is left?  And (if there is something) what do you recommend we do with it?

 

Hemostats: No action needed

 

Inomax: No action needed

 

Terlipressin:  According to Christine, this is 100% R&D budget (I believe the rationale is because it is not yet marketed).  Needs to be discussed with Lawrence Hill

 

Therakos: $150K. 

·         Molly­: please propose what you would suggest we do with a $150K budget.  Tunde is aware of the $143 grant proposals.  Let’s discuss if we want to keep all of them (I suggest not), and which to drop (if any… but I think we should). 

·         Consolidate MWG and ‘other’ costs into one budget

·         Identify what else we need

·         Thumbnail sketch of Publication Plans for clinical trials (Japan study, cGvHD)  Needs to be discussed with Lawrence Hill  

 

 

I think that’s everything, but please let me know if you have any questions or comments. 

 

Best regards,

John

 

John F. Decker,  PhD l Director, Global Scientific Communications
Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals
Perryville III Corporate Park | 53 Frontage Road | Third Floor
P. O. Box 9001 | Hampton, NJ 08827-9001

Subject: FW: Exalgo PI FDA version sent 2-21-12

Dear All,
Please find attached latest FDA version of the EXALGO labeling.  We have several wins and a few losses.  And it looks like FDFA has tracked both their deleted and added text making for ease of review.

As to the additional text proposed for the geriatric sections based on the previously submitted but unlabeled results from the pop-pk study, FDA has requested more time to review.  Their note recommends that we resubmit the proposed text separate from the class REMS and in conjunction with the pending supplement to add the 32mg.

A major win is for the abbreviated boxed warning FDA's agreement to delete their proposed statement on 'instructing patients on proper administration' and adding our text:

Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

An anticipated loss is our attempt to introduce a 75% dose conversion factor.  However, FDA has proposed to move our text on withdrawal to prominence in the bullets associated with the conversion Table 1.

*         Monitor patients for signs or symptoms of opioid withdrawal when converting patients to EXALGO.

Also rejected was our effort to replace dose reductions of 25% with 'a reduced dose', with FDA indicating the statement was not helpful to prescribers and that their proposed reduction was based on PK (albeit IR) data.

Please review closely and let me know if you'd like to meet to discuss.  I'd like to get back to FDA on Friday if at all possible.
Kind regards,
Linda

> Mike & Melissa:
> 
> In looking into to this further, Rachel highlights a subtle discrepancy between the package insert for XARTEMIS XR and ZOHYDRO ER.  If you compare the "Limitations of Use" statements from each, you will see the source of confusion:
> 
> ZOHYDRO ER: "Because of the risks of addiction, abuse, and misuse with opioids, even at recommended doses, and because of the greater risks of overdose and death with extended-release opioid formulations, reserve Zohydro ER for use in patients for whom alternative treatment options (e.g., nonopioid analgesics or immediate-release opioids) are ineffective, not tolerated, or would be otherwise inadequate to provide sufficient management of pain."
> 
> XARTEMIS XR: "Because of the risks of addiction, abuse, misuse, overdose, and death with opioids, even at recommended doses, reserve XARTEMIS XR for use in patients for whom alternative treatment options (e.g., non-opioid analgesics) are ineffective, not tolerated, or would be otherwise inadequate."

> Rachel:

> Would it be possible for you to point me to the specific XARTEMIS XR literature you are referring to so I can look into this further?  I haven't seen the coupons, so I will request one from our Marketing colleagues to better provide guidance on your question below.

> Best regards,
> 
> Tina Purcell, PharmD, PMP | Manager, Medical Affairs Program Management Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals

> 
> Hi Tina,
> 
>      I hope that you are doing well:) I have a question that was brought to my attention from a physician yesterday as an objection. I think that I handled it as best as could be although he was still somewhat questioning. I thought that he was sending out a " smokescreen" until someone else brought it up..Today a PA called me due to a patient's XR script having to be switched due to the patient's concern over the same issue.. On our coupons and literature there is a very pronounced disclaimer regarding risk of abuse, death etc.. This is language that patient's and HCPs are familiar with regarding opioids.. What is articulated a little different that " put off" the physician and now patient is the language regarding how death can occur even if taken as prescribed and after other medicines basically are not adequate.. I understand what this means as someone can obviously die even if taking as prescribed due to various other variables.. Also I and most HCPs understand that an acute opioid is generally written after or when an NSAID etc will not suffice. The language though is strung together in a way though that HCPs have not seen with other opioids.. As for the patient the PA and physician "broke it all down" for them but the death even if taken as prescribed scared them.. I looked at all opioid leave behinds/ coupons as well as Zohydro's warnings and disclaimers and could not find anything like. They were all similar to Exalgo which breaks down for ex why risk of death or abuse.. I am just curious and would like feedback if this comes up again as to why our wording is a little different.. Although  it is saying the same thing as others it is in a more succinct and different manner that can be perceived as, " I risk dying if taking this even as prescribed and it should be last resort". My HCP thought that the language made him appear more liable if someone abuses etc and at a detriment if ever sued because it states clearly that can die and use other medicines first. I get it but what is the reason that our language is "different".. ? I know that they have " tightened" up on opioid labeling but again ours is unique.Sorry if provided too much info. Hopefully it makes sense.. Thanks so much!
> 
> Rachel

Subject: FDA Request - Exalgo Safety Analysis - Allergic Reactions - Sodium Metabisulfite

Commercial colleagues,

I want to make you aware of a recent FDA request for an analysis of the available data (Clinical development and post marketing) for the incidence of allergic reactions (Anaphylaxis, Anaphylactoid, Urticaria, Angioedema, etc.) associated with Exalgo. They have indicated they believe this is attributable to an excipient, Sodium Metabisulfite (See agency letter of request below). This is an important request, and could have significant impact on Exalgo, up to and including labeling change or even reformulation. It is my understanding that sodium metabisulfite is a component of the HM active ingredient rather than the OROS technology (Phil, please correct if I am mistaken). We are working with the agency to identify the appropriate analysis methodology and when they agree, we will conduct the review of data and provide the requested information.

John,

Do we know the potential implication of a request for reformulation with a API source of HM that does not contain sodium metabisulfite? Has a measure of this nature been discussed with our manufacturing partner?

Thanks.

jtp


Please refer to your New Drug Application (NDA) submitted under section 505(b) of the Federal
Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA) for EXALGO (hydromorphone HCl) 8-, 12-, and 16-mg
Extended-Release Tablets.
We also refer to your Periodic Safety Update Reports for Exalgo, received March 8 and June 30,
2011. These reports described cases of anaphylactic shock and pharyngeal edema/urticaria. A
preliminary search of the Adverse Events Reporting System (AERS) also identified cases
suggesting allergic reactions.
Given the occurrence of these cases, and the sodium metabisulfite component in the Exalgo
formulation, we request the following:
Review the Exalgo clinical development program, as well as your postmarket safety surveillance
system, to comprehensively describe cases of allergic reactions and hypersensitivity reactions
that have occurred with Exalgo exposure. This assessment should also include a review of the
medical literature to identify any published cases.
* Provide the proposed search strategy to identify cases to the Division for review prior to
conducting the evaluation.
* The description of the cases from the clinical development program should include a
section with narrative summaries for cases leading to discontinuation and a section with
narrative summaries for cases that qualified as serious adverse events. All cases should be
summarized in tabular form by preferred term, giving the number of cases and incidence
for each treatment arm. Please present data from randomized controlled trials separately
from open label trials.
* Describe separately the experience in the postmarket period. Each case should be
summarized in a narrative summary.

NDA 021217

letter.

Mallinckrodt Controlled Substance Suspicious Order Monitoring
Program

Originator: Page 1 of 4
Karen Harper
Senior Manager, Controlled Substance Compliance


PURPOSE:
In accordance with U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) regulations 21 CFR
1301.74(b), Mallinckrodt has an obligation to inform DEA of suspicious orders.
This procedure outlines the Identification and Review of Peculiar Orders component o f the
Mallinckrodt Suspicious Order Monitoring Program.
APPLIES TO:
Controlled Substance Customer Service Representatives and Managers
Information Service Group
Finance &Administration
Suspicious Order Monitoring Leadership Team
Commercial Group
Controlled Substance Compliance
Security  Director
OVERVIEW:
DEA communication to industry assigns shared responsibility for maintaining appropriate
safeguards against diversion to all registrants.
The Mallinckrodt Controlled Substance Procedure for Identification and Review of Peculiar
Orders, Suspicious  Order Monitoring Program, is designed to:
Define the internal criteria for detecting Peculiar Orders that require further review
Elevate  Peculiar Orders to the level of Suspicious Order as needed, based upon
investigation results, and notification to  DEA  accordingly


   C/S Comp  Identification and Review of Peculiar Orders  2  of 5
3.0  Controlled Substance Compliance Suspicious Order Monitoring Program

DEFINITIONS:
Peculiar Order:  Mallinckrodt direct customer controlled substance order that meets an
internal, established criteria  of 3X the average amount of product ordered
during the previous 12  months by DEA reporting class

Suspicious Order  A Peculiar Order that has been investigated by Finance, Security  Director,
Controlled Substance Compliance without resolution and is elevated to
DEA reportable status
REPORTS REQUIRED
_  Peculiar Order Report
_  Returned 222 Excel Spreadsheet
RESPONSIBILITIES:
Customer Service Representative
Perform the following activities for each controlled substance order:
1. Verify that the account is in good standing  by reviewing the  Do Not Ship List  file on
the Shared Drive

2. Assure that the order is valid  by completing an evaluation and verification of an order to
determine  that the customer has provided a complete order

3. For CI and CII controlled substance orders
 a. Verify customer has provided a complete DEA 222 form
b. Confirm that DEA 222 Purchaser address agrees with customer DEA registration
license
 c. Review the DEA 222 form for any unusual entries  or anomalies
d. Return the 222 form to the customer if it is unacceptable, enter returned 222
information in the  Returned 222 Excel Spreadsheet report
e. Forwards the Returned 222 Excel spreadsheet to Controlled Substance
Compliance monthly
f. Obtain a  Certificate of Available Procurement Quota  from bulk API  customers
using a Manufacturing Registration DEA 222 Form
g  Obtain a  Statement of Intended Use  from customers using a Research,
Compounding Pharmacy, or Analytical Lab registration DEA 222 Form

4. Review the order based on the criteria above and  refer to Controlled Substance
Compliance for additional inve stigation as required

Information Services Department


   C/S Comp  Identification and Review of Peculiar Orders  3  of 5
3.0  Controlled Substance Compliance Suspicious Order Monitoring Program


1.  Programs and publishes the Peculiar Order Report which lists dosage and API orders that
meet the criteria as follows:
a.  Orders in excess of 3X the average amount of product ordered during the previous
12 months  by customer, by DEA reporting class. The algorithms have been
established to identify whether a customer is deviating from a normal order
pattern, and/or increasing in frequency


Finance & Adminstration

1.  Review the IS system generated Peculiar Order Report which lists orders that meet the
established criteria

2.  Annotate Peculiar Order Report accordingly if Finance & Administration review
authorizes shipment with no further investigation, include signature and date reference for
notations

 2a. At the written direction of the Suspicious Order Monitoring Leadership Team,
Peculiar Order investigation is adjusted to address individual
product/order/customer circumstances as needed based upon specific diversion
trends
3a. If input from Commercial Group is required  in the course of Finance &
Administration Peculiar Order review, obtain documentation from Commercial
Group in support of review conclusion

3. Maintains files of Peculiar Order reports and investigation findings for those Pec uliar
Orders that do not require further investigation

1. Refer Peculiar Orders that warrant further investigation to Controlled Substance
Compliance or Security  Director

Commercial Group

Responds to Finance & Administration Group inquiries related to Pec uliar Order Report
investigation. Responses may include recommendations to approve Peculiar Orders for shipment
based upon market knowledge such as receipt of new customer supply agreements or other
justification

Suspicious Order Monitoring Leadership Team

1. Collaborates with Security and Controlled Substance Compliance to adjust Peculiar
Order review based on diversion trends
2.
Consults with Security and Compliance in Monthly Meetings to provide oversight and
guidance for all aspects of the Suspicious Order Monitoring Program

Subject:        FDA Letter-draft content

Draft Content,


Exalgo REMS - Voluntary ETASUs-Development Methodology and Organization

1) Developmental and Continuous Improvement Methodologies

A) After being informed by the agency that the REMS for Exalgo would consist of a MG, Communications Plan and voluntary ETASUs COV/Mallon implemented a evidence based approach, RxFMEA,( failure mode and effects analysis) to define the details of the REMS. This approach is based on a detailed proactive assessment of the medication use and care delivery process related to Exalgo. The RxFMEA application identified specific points where the process could fail

( failure modes). All failures were scored to identify the most hazardous, and the underlying causes were identified.

B) Specific tools were then selected and designed to mitigate the risks of failure. Tools are both educational and enabling in nature and are targeted for use by prescribers, patients, pharmacists and prescriber office staff. Built in redundancy of tools assures at least 2 different stakeholders are targeted for the most hazardous points of failure to ensure more comprehensive risk reduction.

C) Previously invalidated tools are being tested with key stakeholders using a variety of testing methodologies. Revisions will be made based on the testing. Some previously validated tools are being used as is.

D)Continuous improvement will take place via the required and additional voluntary periodic tool assessments and additional RxFMEA analyses at regular intervals post launch. This will likely result in additions, deletions or modifications

to the tools

2) Required REMS Elements-Medication Guide(MG) and Communication Plan(CP)

A) The following required elements will be implemented in the following manner:

1) MGs will be available with Exalgo as part of it's packaging. Specifically, 6 MGs will accompany each bottle of 100 tablets shipped to whosalers and pharmacies. The MG will also:  1)  be contained in the CP, 2) available on 2 Covidien websites( product and safety), 3) carried by sales representatives calling on physicians and retail pharmacies 4) available via a telephone request and a direct mail request system.

2) The CP will consist of the following required elements: Intro letter, PI,MG, Prescriber Brochure and a BRC to request educational and enabling tools. Packages will be direct mailed to the following:

1) all retail and hospital pharmacies ( approx 70,000 recipients)
2) prescribers in our sales rep call plan( approx 13,500 recipients-deciles 5 to 10 of prescribers of LAOs)
3) additional prescribers not in our sales rep call plan( approx 47,000 recipients-deciles 3 and 4 of prescribers of LAOs)

4) relevant Professional Associations( approv 50 recipients)

3) Soon after commercial launch the CP will be repeated to the above audiences.

3) Voluntary Elements to Assure Safe Use( ETASU) -Safe Use Tools

A) The following tools were identified, are being developed and will be provided by Covidien free to charge to stakeholders.

 16 prescriber/office tools
 6 pharmacy tools
 7 patient and caregiver tools

Examples:

1) a non promotional safe use initiative website which will contain information on responsible prescribing, educational information and materials, and downloadable tools.

2) a Clinical Management Brochure which expands on the prescriber brochure and reinforces key safety,

3) a Urine Drug Screen Monograph and primer to assist prescribers in deterring patient opioid naïveté and or compliance.

4) A Patient/Prescriber Medication Agreement( PPMA) to improve physician/patient counseling and appropriate use.

5) a paper dosing diary and 24 hr countdown electronic dosing reminder to help ensure only one dose/day is taken by patients on Exalgo,

6) the APS Clinical Guidelines for Pain Management, Responsible Opioid Prescribing- A Physician's Guide by Scott Fishman to provide educational reference material,

7) the BPI, NRS and ORT to provide prescribers with easy access to validated patient and pain assessment tools.

8) Referral letters in a template format that a PCP could adapt to refer a patient to a pain specialist or a pain specialist could adapt to refer a patient to an addiction specialist.

9) An in- person and Web based training program on responsible opioid prescribing.

10) a patient brochure focused on safe storage, handling and potential disposal of opioids to assist in minimizing theft, misuse or any access by children.

Note: Based on our recent discussions the content of relevant tools will be modified to focus more attention on the safety aspects of higher doses and higher strength tablets.

B) Voluntary Elements to Assure Safe Use( ETASU) -Safe Use Tools-Distribution

1) Prescribers in the 13,500 audience will receive all the prescriber tools at launch via direct mail.
2) Covidien will distribute the prescriber tools to any prescriber once we become aware of Rx activity( see below).

C) Rx Activity Monitoring and Interventions

1) Rx Databases available to Covidien will enable the identification of a prescriber of Exalgo within 21 days after the prescription is dispensed to a patient.

2) If this prescriber is not within  the audience that has received our MG,CP and ETAUS their identification will trigger this to be sent.

3) it will trigger a personal call from a trained Covdien representative to advise the prescriber on the key safety information, available tools, programs, and the potential scheduling of further safety related training or activities.

4) calls and follow-up activities will be triaged to focus on the least experienced physicians prescribing the highest doses first.

D) Assessments and Continuous Improvement

1) The FDA required 6 month, 12 month and annually thereafter assessments will be performed in a robust manner with respect to sample size and stakeholder segment and reported to the agency.

2) Additional market research of tool use and effectiveness are planned in the first 2 years of commercial activity to help ensure a complete picture of tool effectiveness.

3) Covidien will convene a external Safety Advisory Board( SAB) of experts in the field of opioid prescribing, addiction and diversion. This board will meet at least twice yearly to review the data relative to Exalgo utilization, diversion, tool use, and advise Covidien on the need for additional programs related to safe use.

On Apr 26, 2013, at 9:43 AM, "Nosco, Dennis L" <Dennis.Nosco@Covidien.com<mailto:Dennis.Nosco@Covidien.com>> wrote:

Colleagues,

I wanted to share with you a new initiative that Anthony Lassiter and I feel is crucial to moving forward as an independent pharmaceutical company.

That initiative is the creation of a Label Review Committee (LRC).  This committee would be responsible for three major areas:


1)     Driving changes to labels (i.e., package inserts) globally (and, in some cases, regionally) based on new information and/or requests from either internal (e.g., from our Signal Action Committee or other internal sources like the CCSI working group (see below)) or external (e.g., FDA or O-US regulatory agencies) sources.

2)     Approving company core safety information (sometimes referred to as CCDS or CCSI) documents.  These documents, common throughout the pharmaceutical industry but lacking for all but a couple (Optimark and Optiray) of our products, contain the core safety concepts that the company feels should appear in all labels, globally, for a product.   These documents are currently being generated by our relatively newly-formed CCSI working group.  The first one will be ready for approval by the second week in May at the latest.

3)     Helping to ensure alignment of labels (globally) to CCSI content.  This includes aiding, if requested, in addressing questions from local regulatory personnel and/or local regulatory agencies as variations are filed to account for changes due to CCSI content.

Anthony and I have talked through this and we believe that the membership of this committee should be:

Regulatory/Global Labeling: Dennis Nosco, chairperson
Pharmacovigilance: Anthony Lassiter
Legal: Joe Wuestner
Commercial: (business head of area, either Imaging or Specialty Pharma)
Scientific Affairs: Alfredo Bozzini

This committee could also include ad hoc members from other areas (e.g., Regulatory Strategy and CMC Regulatory, PK, Clinical Studies) as their special expertise is needed.

By this e-mail I am asking if all of you would either (a) agree to be on this committee or (b) designate someone from your area to be the representative on this committee.

Once I get agreement as to membership I will call our first meeting.  The timing of formation of this committee is crucial as we have our first new CCSI document that is about ready to be submitted to the LRC for review.  In addition, we have a company initiative regarding EXALGO labeling and inclusion of abuse deterrent safety language that will require this committee s input on language and help on getting these changes implemented globally)

As timing is short to get this committee operational please get back to me AND Anthony with any questions you have.  I would like to set up our first meeting for sometime in the next 3 weeks.

  Subject: RE: Caraco 






  Sun Pharmaceuticals and Caraco overview (November 2011) 
  INS NSP data is attached to the email for your review 


  1. API - In November 2008 Sun Pharmaceuticals acquired 100% ownership of chattem chemicals, Inc 
  from Elcat, Inc. chattem was a narcotic importer for methamphetamine, phenylacetone, raw opium and 
  concentrate poppy straw. They are licensed by the DEA to manufacture schedule 1 to 5 controlled 
  substances. For the year ending 2008, chattem was estimated to have sales of USD 26 million. In a 
  recent company earnings release, sun called out an 8% increase in the API facility revenue as well as 
  bringing 5 new API products on-line in 2011. company press releases state that the cranbury' NJ 
  manufacturing facility (the old Able Labs) sources its API from the chattem API plant for controlled 
  substances. 



  Z. DOSAGE MANUFACTURING - In 2005 Sun Pharmaceuticals acquired the site in cranbury, NJ (the old 
  Able Labs that was in Bankruptcy court} which was authorized to manufacture finished dosage forms for 
  controlled substances. This is named by sun as their only site in the us authorized to manufacture 
  finished dosage forms of controlled substances. Products manufactured at the cranbury' NJ plant include 
  HYCD-APAP, Promethazine and oxycodone. There are at least two other controlled substances 
  manufactured there - I believe these may be codeine APAP and ADHD medications. 



  In August 2010, Sun received an FDA warning letter for the Cranbury facility; the FDA reinspected in 
  June 2011 and a press release in September 2011 stated all issues had been resolved. In reviewing the 
  483 associated with the warning letter, there were citations involving gemfibrozil, promethazine, 
  oxycodone (broken tablets and repackaging quality issues) as well as one mention of stability data issues 
  for certain lots of HYCD-APAP from I2/08-12/09. 



  a. I noted per the INS NSP data that oxycodone HCL shipments out began in August 2011 and escalated 
  in September of 2011; the October 2011 data shows shipment of 2.8 million tablets for all three strengths 
  (~2.0 million were the 30 mg). They are shipping 5 mg, 15 mg and 30 mg strengths. It appears to have 
  taken them about 3 months to get back up to near pre-interruption capacity. sun pharma mentioned in some 
  of their documents that they would be bringing back products a few at a time and that ramp-up to full 
  capacity would happen slowly. 



  b. I also noted that there was a similar ramp-up of Codeine-Promethazine in the September-October 
  timeframe in the INS NSP data. 



  c. Finally, INS NSP data shipments of the HYCD-APAP 5-325 strength have begun as of October 2011 
  (220,000 tablets). The other strengths (7.5-325, I0-325 and 10-660) have not yet begun shipping as of 
  October 2011 NSP data. My estimate is that they will be back up to full capacity by the end of January 
  for HYCD-APAP with all 325 mg strengths. I question whether they will bother with the I0-660 as the 
  volume was not significant prior to interruption. 



  3. CARACO - Caraco (now a wholly owned subsidiary of sun Pharmaceuticals) distributes controlled 
  substances for sun Pharmaceuticals including HYCD APAP, Promethazine and Roxicodone (oxycodone HCL). 
  They also have their own manufacturing facility which is currently under consent decree and is not 
  manufacturing. The only pain-related product manufactured in the Detroit facility was Tramadol (not a 
  controlled substance). several publically available news articles implied that certain AmoAs were being 
  transferred to the Cranbury Facility in order that they might continue shipping products; specifically 
  10-12 Amoxs. In looking at the INS data there are certain products that have not dropped off in the NSP 
  data or have already returned to pre-consent decree levels (METOPROLOL TART, METFORMIN HCL, CITALOPRAM 
  HBR, TRAMADOL HCL, ELIXOPHYLLIN, ISOSORBIDE DINITRA, BENZONATATE, NIMODIPINE, ZOLPIDEM TART, CD/PROMETH, 
  SYNALGOS DC, CLONAZEPAM). My assumption would be that these had either been transferred to the Cranbury 
  facility or another contract manufacturer in order to prevent disruption of supply.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
Date: June 15, 2010
Contact: Rich Isaacson
Number: (313) 234-4310

Michigan Pharmaceutical Supplier S Dea License Suspended
-Harvard Drug Group, LLC distributed 13 million doses of Oxy from 2008-2010

JUN 15 -- (Detroit, MI)   Robert L. Corso, Special Agent in Charge of the Detroit Field Division, Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) announced today the Immediate Suspension of the Federal Controlled Substance Registration of Harvard Drug Group, LLC.

Harvard Drug Group, LLC, based in Livonia, Michigan, has been the subject of a DEA investigation that alleges the company was selling large quantities of controlled substances to pharmacies, primarily in Florida. The investigation has revealed that several of Harvard s largest purchasers of oxycodone were engaged in schemes to dispense controlled substances based on prescriptions that were written for other than legitimate medical purposes. The investigation revealed that Harvard Drug Group, LLC, distributed over 13 million dosage units of oxycodone products to customers in the two year time frame between March 2008 and March 2010.

Robert L. Corso, stated,  Pharmaceutical companies have a responsibility to ensure that the drugs they sell don t end up in the hands of drug traffickers or businesses that are conducting their business illegally. Harvard Drug Group, LLC, should have known, based on the large, frequent quantities, that their customers were diverting oxycodone into arenas that were not legitimate. Today s action sends the message that the DEA is working hard to hold accountable those companies that are operating in a manner outside of federal law.

DEA s action suspends Harvard Drug Group, LLC s DEA Certificate of Registration in accordance with an Immediate Suspension Order and pursuant to Sections 303 and 304 of the Controlled Substances Act, Title 21, Sections 823 and 824. The DEA s investigation of Harvard Drug Group, LLC, has determined that the continued registration of this company constitutes an imminent danger to public health and safety.

Harvard Drug Group, LLC. received written notice of the factual and legal basis for this action. In addition, Harvard Drug Group, LLC will be given an opportunity for an administrative hearing within the next 60 days. After the hearing, the DEA Deputy Administrator will make a final decision on whether Harvard Drug Group, LLC registration should be permanently revoked. This decision will be published in the Federal Register.

Oxycodone is the generic name of an addictive prescription painkiller that is classified under federal narcotics laws as a Schedule II controlled substance. Oxycodone is typically legally prescribed to combat acute, severe pain for legitimate medical purposes. Accordingly, these prescriptions are usually for a modest number of pills to be taken over a short period of time.

This is an ongoing investigation. Please forward any questions to DEA Detroit Public Information Officer Rich Isaacson at (313) 234-4310.

Concept for slides are as follows:

 

Category 4 studies

1. They use outcomes that provide meaningful measures of abuse deterrence.

2. They produce estimates of abuse deterrence that are nationally representative, or are 548 based on data from a large geographic region.

3. They assess overall and route-specific abuse and abuse deterrence.

4. They are sufficiently powered to assess meaningful changes in drug abuse.

 

Tier 4

Claims that a Product has Demonstrated Reduced Abuse in the Community

 

Issue: strategy for assessing abuse reduction for a small market product has not been validated. Prospective data collection (example, registry) is not well suited for studying abuse over extended periods of time.

 

Exalgo Tier 4 experience

 

Inflexxion is known and respected by FDA

NaviPPro data can be readily studies retrospectively. Number of comparator drugs is robust and representative of the abusing population

Exalgo Category 4 epidemiological study completed in 3-4 months; cost $600k

 

Plan

Retrospective matched cohort epidemiological study conducted in the NaviPPro database at three years post launch.

<image001.png>

 
Estimate Changes

 
Mallinckrodt plc

 
We maintain our SELL rating and $34PT, which we arrive at via two valuation methods: a 7.1x multiple on our 2013 EBITDA estimate of $382 million, and a P/E multiple (11.6x our CY13 EPS estimate of $2.92). We believe MNK s current premium valuation is NOT warranted, as we think F 14 sales and earnings are likely to fall as a result of increased competition within its pharmaceutical segment. Key products (generic Concerta and Exalgo) are expected to face competition, likely leading to a fall in sales and profits beginning in the first quarter of F 14. While the Company updated its F 13 financial guidance to reflect sales growth of 8-10% (from 7-11%), with specialty pharma segment sales growth of 22-25% (from 21-25%), and medical imaging sales declines of -5 to -8% (from -3 to -7%). We believe F 14 financial guidance (expected to be announced by the end of October) could be far less robust. In F 14, we expect sales declines for generic Concerta and branded Exalgo, as generic competition enters. In addition, with the Company preparing for a potential approval and launch of MNK-795 (an extended-release hydrocodone / acetaminophen combo product with abuse deterrent technology for the relief of acute, moderate to severe pain), we believe SG&A costs are likely to increase. On last Friday s call, management indicated its plans to expand its current 200-person sales force by 50-100%. As a result, we have increased our annual SG&A cost estimates by ~$45 million/year.

 

Lowering F 13-F 16 EPS forecasts to $2.89, $2.27, $2.50, and $2.75, from $3.18, $2.61, $2.73, and $2.87, respectively. We have increased our F 14-F 16 revenue forecasts to reflect a greater contribution from its two new drug pipeline products, MNK-795 and MNK-155, both abuse deterrent formulations of acetaminophen containing combination pain products. Combined, our new F 13-F 15 estimates include sales of $25 million, $120 million, and $200 million, up from $10 million, $60 million, and $80 million, respectively. While MNK-795 was recently granted a priority review, we believe much is riding on the Company s ability to garner an abuse-deterrent label. While management indicated on its call that it feels it has done all of the necessary pre-clinical and clinical work to garner such a label, we believe the FDA s decision here is an upcoming binary event, which could have a significant impact on MNK s share price.

 

Investment Summary   SELL/$34PT. We maintain our SELL rating and $34PT, which we arrive at via two valuation methods, a 7.1x multiple on our 2013 EBITDA est. of $382 million, and a P/E multiple (11.6x our CY13 EPS estimate of $2.92). MNK shares currently trade at 15.5x our new CY13 EPS estimate of $2.92, and 19.9x our new CY14 EPS estimate of $2.28. On average, we believe MNK shares are trading at a 58% premium to its peers on a forward P/E multiple basis. Based on our expectations for MNK to face additional competition on several of its key pharmaceutical products (generic Concerta, and Exalgo) in the second half of 2013, we believe F 14 revenue could fall approximately (4.6%) vs. F 13, with EPS dropping to $2.27 (21% YOY) in F 14. With F 14 expected to be a transition year, we believe MNK shares could drop 25% from current levels.

From: Spaulding, Eileen L. [mailto:Eileen.Spaulding@covidien.com]
Sent: Tuesday, September 07, 2010 10:45 AM
To: White, Heather R.
Subject: Crossroads Recovery DEA Reg# RC0270974



 

Heather,


 


Attached is supporting documentation of suspicious activity we have discovered surrounding the sale of Crossroads Recovery, Inc. in Dallas, TX with the following details for your consideration:


 


·         Controlled Substance Compliance was notified by our credit department that customer Crossroads Recovery, Dallas TX (DEA Reg# RC0270974) had an outstanding bill that was in dispute between the old owners of the NTP clinic and the new owners of clinic from February 2010. 

·         The clinic was sold by Diane Day and purchased by Joseph Baiamonte and Frances McGrady.  The sales contract is dated February 15, 2010.  Attached is a letter from the new owners with specific pages from the sales contract, it is not inclusive.  Cover letter provided by the purchasers state that they did not close on the sales contract until February 19, 2010 and that they were not responsible for any fees until March 1, 2010. 

·        A letter was sent to Mallinckrodt on march 8, 2010 from Diane Day (attached) updating Joseph Baiamonte and Francis McGrady as being authorized to order and receive methadone, however it does not state that the clinic was sold or transferred ownership.  Thus, we did not change any of our accounts as the current DEA Registration for Crossroads Recovery was in effect until August 31, 2010 and we simply thought they were updating their authorized signors list.

·         Attached are also copies of 2 different 222 forms, one from February and one from March.  The March invoice has been paid, the February invoice has not and was the cause for the sale to be brought to our attention.  Based on the signature of the sales contract it appears that Diane Day did sign the 222 form from February 17, 2010, however it appears that someone else could have potentially signed Diane Day's name on the March 222 form with their initials after her name.  Mallinckrodt continued to ship at this time as we had not been made aware of the change of ownership and 222 used to order was for the same DEA Reg# RC0270974 currently on file.

·         A review of shipping records from March 1, 2010 to date, shows 4 orders have been shipped, all using the DEA Reg# RC0270974 and sequential DEA Form 222 numbers.  The March order was signed with the name Diane Day and the subsequent 3 orders (May, June, August) were signed by Lillian Williams McGrady.

As part of our ongoing Suspicious Order Monitoring program, Mallinckrodt will be incorporating the requirement for any clinic to provide proof of ownership and/or sale immediately upon notification to us of the sale of a NTP clinic.


 


Please do not hesitate to contact me if I can provide further information or any assistance.


 


Regards,

_____________________________________________
From:   Nelson, Lee 
Sent:   February 14, 2008 6:30 PM
To:     Wilkening, Gary; Leonard, John
Cc:     Nicholl, Harry; Treadaway, Joan; Harper, Karen; Wynne, Mike F; Stewart, Bill
Subject:        RE: Simple and Complex Quota models

Gary,

Hydrocodone is mid-level complex.  It has only one input - Codeine - and one output - 1582 hydrocodone bitartrate.  It is a good example of straight-line production with short recycles.

Morphine has everything you mentioned below, but has 2 quotas, raw materials from 3 countries, 5 charging points, 7 isolated intermediates, multiple assay intermediate (M&C), and besides 2 sales products is converted to 6 other synthetic products.  Also after it is converted, there are derivative streams which come back into inventory and need their own WIP.

Opium/CPS receipts are simple, but they have multiple assays and 19 year-end reports.

Maybe Morphine and Opium/CPS should be added as Extra Complex!

Lee

_____________________________________________
From:   Wilkening, Gary 
Sent:   February 14, 2008 3:43 PM
To:     Nelson, Lee; Leonard, John
Cc:     Nicholl, Harry; Treadaway, Joan; Harper, Karen; Wynne, Mike F; Stewart, Bill
Subject:        RE: Simple and Complex Quota models

John Leonard and I talked and if you have not picked a complex item, you may want to use Hydrocodone.

Hydrocodone Alkaloid (6282) gets made from Codeine.
There are waste streams from the process that contain Hydrocodone Alkaloid and affect Quota.
Hydrocodone Alkaloid has a recycle stream that goes to another process that gets converted to another product 3959 (Recovered Hydrocodone Alkaloid).

A portion of this gets reprocessed back into 3959 because the impurities are too high to process forward.  This process is done in Building 235 and 6&7.

Hydrocodone Alkaloid is converted to Hydrocodone Bitartrate which has a conversion factor to adjust it back to Alkaloid.

There is also a recycle stream from this which goes back to be recovered as Hydrocodone Alkaloid Code 3959.

There may also be other items that I am missing.

Thanks

Gary




_____________________________________________
From:   Nelson, Lee 
Sent:   February 14, 2008 1:51 PM
To:     Leonard, John
Cc:     Nicholl, Harry; Treadaway, Joan; Wilkening, Gary; Harper, Karen; Nelson, Lee; Wynne, Mike F; Stewart, Bill
Subject:        Simple and Complex Quota models

John,

You have the meeting set for Monday 2/18 which is a vacation day.
 << File: DEA St. Louis Quota model.xls >>
The simple manufacturing quota model is 3221 Aminonitrile.

This product has only one step, one use, no WIP and is very seldom reworked.

Quota procedure
Add all R and PR Receipt transactions
Add Issue transactions only if the work order code is the same as the charging code.
        3221 --> 3221

The net is quota consumed

MC9382 - step 1
Batch Records
6.110 - Aminonitrile Drying
6.120 Rework of Aminonitrile.
Quota: QC9254 Methadone Intermediate

Sincerely,
Lee Nelson

As we discussed last Friday, demand for API products manufactured at the St. Louis Plant is increasing significantly.

Carla and I have a meeting later this week with Nick Litzsinger and Marc Montgomery to line out how to capture opportunistic API business in quota requests so that we can offer our full support to these growth initiatives by obtaining quota appropriately.

Eric Evans has expressed a desire to meet with DEA and present our short term and longer term business strategies to the agency.

To give you a bit of background on this, DEA requires the following designations for quota requests:

         Commercial Manufacturing

         Product Development

         Packaging/Labeling

         Replacement

         Transfer

 

The Product Development dropdown instruction box on the DEA electronic form states: 

(Product Development)  Efforts such as laboratory scale, exhibit batches, etc.  Note:  validation batches or other validation efforts in which the manufactured material may be commercially sold should be requested under Commercial Manufacturing  (category)

These orders hit the "threshold limit". I will probably butcher this, but here goes:

multiplied by 3. this is called the "target average qty", which is an acceptable amou nt. Keep in mind
they are measured by molecule of the product family and not on skus.

molecule)
The "target average qty" for morphine is 960, actual order qty is 1392 (molecules again)

*       Completed job description for Webster Groves Training Coordinator.  This is a newly created function at Webster Groves and apparently it is now required that every salaried person submit a job description.  This is a Quality next step from an FDA inspection at Hobart (so I'm told)..

Gillies addressed - I'm not sure who all attended - but the point of the meeting was to stress the importance of using badges and security at Hazelwood correctly.  Bob Schaefer said that he thinks there is a very nonchalant attitude toward security at Hazelwood.  Bob said he would like John Gillies to come to Webster to do the same thing.             bldg. 5 for a st. Louis plant end-user (such as Jonathan Rowland), the box is opened by bldg. 5 so the packing list can be checked to see who the sample goes to.  The issue is that the sample is not check-weighed, or if it is, no sample transfer form is filled out by bldg. 5. The complaint from Jonathan is that Bldg. 5 insists that the person delivering a sample to them verifies and records the weights, but bldg. 5 will not do the same when a sample is being received from them.  The sample has been handled and compromised before it gets to the end building.

Jerry,

DEA has begun requiring that bulk manufacturers supply the specific customer ship to DEA registration as part of the quota justification process, which is likely driving the JDE requirement.

DEA has actually begun comparing our dosage customers' procurement quota requests against Mallinckrodt's bulk manufacturing quota requests. 

There have been times that DEA has told us they are not granting a bulk manufacturing quota request in full because our stated customer has not applied for and/or received procurement quota.

When DEA implemented the requirement for customer specific DEA registration numbers on quota requests, they indicated that the information became necessary due to innovations in the manufacturing supply chain such as external manufacturers, 3rd party manufacturers, joint ventures.  Further, they admitted that they could not keep it all straight.

An example of a current quota request back-up sheet that we submitted to DEA for Oxycodone bulk manufacturing quota has been copied below, as you can see the Oxycodone sales from Mallinckrodt St. Louis are forecasted for both Mallinckrodt Hobart and Mikart for Mallinckrodt manufacture.

Below are my initial thoughts.  It may be helpful to discuss some of
this live. 

If I understand the project correctly, the intent is to provide a
decision support tool / algorithm that can drive appropriate opioid
selection, by providing education on important pharmacologic differences
in opioid agents.  While I agree fully with a simplified approach, we
can't assume that prescribers understand the basic principles and thus,
it is important to not oversimplify the tool.   I think this can be a
valuable tool for opioid prescribers and believe that we should include
the level of detail that will have the greatest impact. 

In its current format, the algorithm may be confusing to prescribers.
Consider adding additional information to clarify 'when and why' an
alternative opioid may be appropriate.  For example, a patient may be a
"partial responder" to a specific medication and/or have unacceptable
adverse effects, at which point a change in therapy would be
appropriate.  Additionally, the patient may be a "partial responder"
with no adverse effects and a change in therapy may also be appropriate,
but for a different reason.  On the other hand, the "partial response"
could be the result of a subtherapeutic dose, at which point an increase
in dose on the current therapy may be sufficient.  The only perspective
reflected in the current algorithm (on the hydrocodone side) is that a
"partial response" is the result of inferior potency (designated by the
X) and the solution is hydromorphone.  

Adding a few key decision points will help provide a more useful tool to
providers.  In its current format, the algorithm doesn't provide enough
information or decision points to explain why, for example, a "partial
responder" would be best transitioned to "specific named opioid".  As I
stated above,  a partial response could be the result of many things
(subtherapeutic dose, drug -drug interaction, receptor variability, etc)
all of which have a different solution.  Likewise, I would suggest the
same level of detail for "responder" and "non-responder"
recommendations.  Responsible clinicians should not and typically will
not select or prescribe a specific opioid, based on limited guidance
such as "partial response" or "no response".  I think we have to modify
the algorithm to align with what a clinician should and typically will
consider in making an opioid selection decision.  With those additional
decision points, the algorithm can become a useful tool to providers.

Additional points to consider about the current diagram:  
*	Consider adding information to clarify why we have only included
the opioids listed.  I believe you are focusing on a transition from the
available short-acting combination products (e.g., HC/APAP and OC/APAP).

*	There is a triangle in the key that is followed by the statement
"Oxymorphone makes very little contribution to analgesic activity;
oxycodone produces most of the analgesic effect".  As written, this
statement is incorrect as oxymorphone produces most of the analgesia
associated with oxycodone (e.g., a non-responder / partial responder to
oxycodone may not be fully metabolizing oxycodone to its more active
metabolite).  In that case a dose increase (if no intolerable side
effects) or a change in therapy may be appropriate.  
*	The left side of the diagram (hydrocodone) has an option for
"responder" but the right side does not.  This could be perceived as
bias towards hydromorphone.  A "responder" on SA oxycodone (e.g.,
Percocet) would likely be transitioned to "oxycontin" first if an ER
formulation is appropriate.  
*	The left side of the diagram indicates that if a patient does
not respond to HM then oxymorphone is the appropriate treatment choice
(dotted line) .  It would be more appropriate to state "consider
different opioid" - oxymorphone may or may not be the next appropriate
choice.   For example, if the patient has liver dysfunction, oxymorphone
may be the least appropriate choice.  Same for the other said - if "does
not respond" to oxymorphone, hydromorphone may or may not be the next
appropriate choice.

    "Fraley, Tamara" <tamara.fraley@mallinckrodt.com>


Terry  

 

Below is a summation of the 5:30pm group. 2 PCPs (1 internist   geriatrics), 1 Physiatrist

Reaction to Messages

Dosing

Two physicians were most motivated by the message  two tablets, twice daily for fast-acting and long-lasting relief   felt it was the most succinct and to the point

The other physician liked the message about the 12 hour dosing not requiring their patients to watch the clock, chase their pain, etc   felt an emotional appeal to this message

pK

All respondents were motivated by messages related to the steady and sustained plasma concentrations with fewer peaks and troughs, again paired with the pK graph   Liked that it was concise and to the point and felt the graph was very helpful

Efficacy

One physician motivated by the message first and only (which tells them it is unique) .with immediate and extended release properties fast acting and long lasting- they found the fast acting and long lasting clever

Another liked the message about XARTEMIS XR lasting longer allowing the patients to focus on healing and recovery

The last physician connected to the more emotional messaging related to the Harris Poll statistic about the number of acute pain suffers have to wake in the night to dose

Patient type

Two were motivated by the message with XARTEMIS XR being suited for patients with pain throughout the day and night for whom you typically prescribe Percocet

The other physician was motivated by the message indicating the acute pain often lasts throughout the day and night and it is well suited to a product that is both fast acting and long lasting

Abuse

One physician was motivated by the message about XARTEMIS XR meeting 3 primary endpoints   although this caused a lot of questions related to the results

Another physician felt the message about receiving priority review was the most motivating

Dear AfBPM Responsible/Safe Use Working Group Members:
Thank you for your participation in our call on Thursday, October 15. We appreciate your time and efforts.
