AfBPM Responsible/Safe Use Working Group Call Recap
Participants: Shaina Smith (U.S. Pain Foundation); James Appleby and Trish D'Antonio (The Gerontological
Society of America); Wade Delk (American Society for Pain Management Nursing); Lisa Winstel (Caregiver
Action Network); Marcia Lee Taylor (Partnership for Drug-Free Kids); Kevin Webb and Rhonda Sciarra
(Mallinckrodt); Green Room

•

•

•

Access survey officially closed on October 5 with 833 completed responses; trends and key takeaways
remain the same as previously reported, most notable that while opioids have been most commonly
recommended by HCPs for the management of pain they have also been the most difficult to access;
results currently being weighted by survey experts
On the first day of the Summit (Thurs, November 12), KWebb will open Summit and Green Room will
introduce speakers, which will be followed by speaker presentations, review of current literature on pain
management, working/networking lunch and Working Group breakouts
o In terms of speakers we are currently looking at Dr. Howard Koh for responsible/safe use
(involved with recent National. Action. Plan for Adverse Drug Event Prevention) and Dr.
Nalamachu for access; UPDATE: following 10/15 Working Group call Lynn DeBar notified
Green Room that she is unavailable to speak at the Summit due to scheduling
Group discussed potential AfBPM tactics:
o LWinstel: The transition of care is important as not everyone is close to their hospital in terms of
distance; caregivers need to better understand how to take care of their loved ones once they are
home; a discharge protocol for properly managing pain would be useful with instructions for the
caregiver included
o TD'Antonio: It's important to integrate caregivers into the entire discharge process and equip
them with the right tools
o WDelk: Is there a way to capture what pain management medication can potentially do and their
side-effects, including information about opioids and alternatives to seek relief?

MNKOI 0001017680

 •

•
•
•
•

•

WDelk shared the Checklist at a meeting last month and noted it was very well-received
and copies were requested
o MTaylor: Sports injuries are critical with regard to pain management and important to note that
often parents allow their children to manage their own pain/medication; need to consider
addressing concept of people managing their medicine and ensuring a responsible caregiver is
available to manage process, keep medication in a safe place, etc.
o JAppleby: Communication to patients and caregivers about the affects of opioids on other
systems in the body is important, e.g.,opioid-induced constipation (OIC), particularly for the
aging population; could be included as part of the discharge plan
o LWinstel: One of the more difficult topics to speak about is intimacy and how OIC can affect it
o KWebb: All of the ideas discussed have merit as we think through under the context of
continuing to ensure patient safety and not doing anything that would prevent access to
appropriate pain management; important to remember that we don't want to go too far down one
path; need to factor in empowerment of the patient and caregiver to have conversations with
healthcare professionals and continue to focus on individualized patient care; could also
highlight what about opioids patients needs to know when they are leaving the hospital with
these medications
o JAppleby: Patients and caregivers are likely not asking all of the right questions about pain
management in advance of surgical procedures, accidents, etc., and some patients have to
remember they are high-risk
o KWebb: There is currently a receptive environment due to the National Pain Strategy and other
initiatives re: individual patient care and patient safety; if we can advance a tool that allows us to
tap into this already-receptive audience we may get more traction
Any members with additional tactics/initiatives for consideration, please send them to
gsherman@greenroompr.com
Like last year, we are considering inviting non-Alliance members to attend and participate in the
Summit; a memo will be forthcoming week of 10/19 with additional information (completed)
It's critical that all AfBPM members RSVP to the Summit (via the invitation that went on 10/7) by
10/21; hotel accommodations must be secured by 10/23
In terms of media activities a press release will be issued by AfBPM on 11/17 and trade and consumer
media outreach will ensue; if AfBPM members have media contacts/established relationships with either
trade or consumer media outlets please email gshermanqD,greenroompr.com with the information so that
we can add these folks to our media lists
Dr. Nalamachu, who work with the Alliance for Patient Access, authored a blog post on behalf of
AfBPM which has been submitted to FormularyWatch blog; acceptance status is pending

Participants: Charlotte/National Alliance for Caregiving; Bob Twillman (American Academy of Pain
Management); Kevin Webb and Rhonda Sciarra (Mallinckrodt); Green. Room

•

management, working/networking lunch and Working Group breakouts
o In terms of speakers we are currently looking at Dr. Howard Koh for responsible/safe use
(involved with recent National Action Plan for Adverse Drug Event Prevention) and Dr.

MNKOI 0001017681

 •

•

•
•

•

Nalamachu for access; UPDATE: following 10/15 Working Group call Lynn DeBar notified
Green Room that she is unavailable to speak at the Summit due to scheduling
o BTwillman: Linda Porter and Dave Thomas could be speakers for consideration; BTwillman
happy to forward letter on behalf of AfBPM if needed
Group discussed potential AfBPM tactics:
o BTwillman: Any kind of emphasis on educating prescribers about how to work with pharmacists
so that the patient doesn't get caught in the middle and end up without a prescription is critical;
there is tension right now between pharmacists and prescribers as pharmacists are not getting
what they need from prescribers; pharmacists need to ensure the prescriptions they are filling for
opioids are legitimate and have to call prescribers about the patient, diagnosis, etc.; prescribers
don't have time, feel judged, etc.; pharmacists may end up not feeling comfortable fi lling the
opioid prescriptions if they are not getting the information they need; this could potentially
prevent patients from getting opioid prescriptions filled in that chain pharmacy; new draft
guidance for pharmacists from the Florida Board of Pharmacy that addresses this issue has been
release; BTwillman to share document with Green Room
o Green Room: Perhaps AfBPM can consider a checklist or questionnaire physicians can fill out or
some kind of electronic information exchange so that nurses are equipped to speak to
pharmacists when they call
o Charlotte: Caregivers often may not know that there is a backstage conversation happening
between prescribers and pharmacists and don't feel empowered themselves to question what the
hold up is; there needs to be some sort of tool to facilitate the transaction more effectively
o Green Room: Perhaps we consider a series of patient, provider or pharmacist features and try to
reach out to reporters with those stories
Any members with additional tactics/initiatives for consideration, please send them to

Subject:        Update on mystery "Oxycodone 30 mg" tablets

Hi Karen and Bill,

After preliminary investigation by CAR using non-destructive methods, we can state without doubt that the tablets received from Hobart did not originate from Mallinckrodt.

The markings on the mystery tablet are very similar, but when examined under a microscope they are clearly not identical to Mallinckrodt tooling used for 30 mg Oxycodone tablets.
The mystery tablets are made of completely different ingredients when compared with the Mallinckrodt Oxycodone 30 mg tablet.
The mystery tablets do not appear to contain any oxycodone (this will be confirmed this week).
The mystery tablets are slightly larger than Mallinckrodt Oxycodone 30 mg tablets.



As I mentioned, these tests were non-destructive. Over the next couple of days, we will be running the validated analytical method to test for the presence of oxycodone.

We currently suspect that the unknown tablets contain some type of drug and we are working to identify that drug is and will provide a report to you later this week.

March 28, 2014

By HEALTH NEWS FLORIDA STAFF

On both Florida coasts, the toll of oxycodone continues, as a doctor is arrested and clinic owners are convicted.

 

The Boca Raton Police arrested Dr. Harry Kesten, 47, owner of Quick Test Labs in Delray Beach, after he tried to buy $300 worth of oxycodone pills, the South Florida Sun Sentinel reports. Police used an undercover informant to tape a phone conversation, then set up the fake buy.

 

In the recorded call, according to the arrest report, Kesten said he could falsify drug test results and make fake labels for prescription bottles.

 

Meanwhile in Tampa, in a case that took years to bring to trial, a jury convicted the operators of First Medical Group pain clinic of trafficking in oxycodone as well as conspiracy, the Tampa Bay Times reports.

 

Those who were convicted after five days of jury deliberation were clinic owners Jorge Gonzalez-Betancourt, 53, and Michele Gonzalez, 37, both of Tampa, and manager was Maureen Altman, 58, of Lakeland.

 

The clinic's physician, Dr. Kimberly Daffern, died in 2011 before the case went to trial. As the Times reports, he was accused of prescribing 1 million oxycodone pills in three months.

 

Even though the clinic attracted hordes of customers from as far as Ohio and Kentucky, it took years of investigation for years before prosecutors felt there was enough evidence to go to trial.

 

It is notoriously difficult to prosecute drug cases involving prescription drugs. Last month, the three-month-long trial of a Palm Beach County physician and pharmacist ended in acquittal. Dr. Timothy Sigman and pharmacist Peter Del Toro had been charged with dealing in human growth hormone, testosterone and anabolic steroids.

Hi Maggie,

 

I’ve attached the policy analysis that has been prepared on the Massachusetts legislation.  Note, that it is effective immediately (rather than late 2015 as you note), but there will be a host of rulemaking that will need to be done.  From a Policy / Government Affairs perspective, we’ll be actively engaged in the process.

 

Please note that there is still further analysis that needs to be done by our Legal and Regulatory teams before we assess potential benefit to our current portfolio (i.e. Exalgo & Xartemis) as well as MNK-155.  There is a school of thought that the language around ADT determination is so narrow that the data that we’ve (MNK) generated as part of the past submissions to the FDA would not be sufficient for the Drug Formulary Commission to make an “abuse deterrent” determination. 


As such, we should not engage with any customers around this.  We’ll keep all posted as more information is gathered, analysis prepared, and an official MNK position is developed around this legislation.  Further, I ask that this analysis not be shared beyond this group (above) and, especially, externally.

 

Happy to further discuss.  Hope all is well-


Best,


Derek

Subject: pending MA legislation



 

Hi Derek

I’m am in our Managed Markets group and have responsibility for some national health plans and the regional plans in New England and upstate NY. The Boston Globe ran an article on August 1st regarding the MA legislature’s approval on an opioid bill. There are several provisions in the bill related to preventing and treating substance abuse.

Specific to prescription meds, the legislation “seeks to encourage the use of certain kinds of painkillers that are less likely to be used inappropriately by addicts. Unless directed otherwise by a physician, pharmacists would be required to dispense drugs formulated to prevent abuse, such as those that cannot be crushed for injection or snorting. Insurers would be barred from charging higher copayments on those drugs”

The legislation doesn’t take effect until late 2015 but I’m wondering if we can leverage this with the payers in MA and possibly hospital systems. Also, I thought that CT had some bills pending on something similar but can’t find anything on the CT government website. Any ideas you may have on how I can approach payers and key thought leaders in the medical community would be much appreciated. Thanks in advance-

On Feb 26, 2013, at 8:19 AM, "Nichols, Bill" <Bill.Nichols@Covidien.com<mailto:Bill.Nichols@Covidien.com>> wrote:

No problem at all. We still have the responsibility to make things happen and are working toward solutions.



On Feb 26, 2013, at 8:43 AM, "Wickline, Ronald P" <Ronald.Wickline@covidien.com<mailto:Ronald.Wickline@covidien.com>> wrote:

Do you mind if I share these with Jamie?

Sent from my iPad

On Feb 25, 2013, at 10:02 PM, "Nichols, Bill" <Bill.Nichols@Covidien.com<mailto:Bill.Nichols@Covidien.com>> wrote:

Sorry for the delayed response. I conducted interviews this afternoon then flew up to Atlanta this evening.

I hear a number of things as I talk to DMs and work in the field. I can put together a more formal response, but here are some items in no particular order:


1.    A certain degree of disruption with the realignment   some more than others. I tend to forget about that but the DMs quickly remind me that reps are still learning some new targets   again, some more than others. That will show when we see numbers for frequency.

2.    While most reps are able to get access with most targets, getting access at our desired frequency can be a challenge especially where lunch appointments are a requirement.

3.    Overall regulatory climate for opioids is deteriorating. I know we don t want to acknowledge that, but I hear it more and more when I work with reps. It s not always in the form of new legislation. In Louisiana, for example, it is a new investigator for the LA Board of Medical Examiners. Here is a quote from Jerry from his latest report to me on this   Apparently she is  heavily against the prescribing of opioids and believes that all pain patients should be treated with NSAIDs , injections and physical therapy. She has gone head to head with many of my physicians arguing that there are no studies demonstrating opioids as being effective in managing long term chronic pain. She utilizes intimidation going into their offices sometimes monthly  combing  thru their files and forcing them to document their discussions sending them back to her in what she calls a  memorial  of their discussion. She has recently informed two of my physicians that they can only write one opioid for a patient. The physicians say that she cannot legally do this but at the same time they do not want her back in their office next month. One of my physicians had a patient controlled on 32 mg of Exalgo with hydrocodone for breakthrough. When he told her that he could now only prescribe one of the two she chose hydrocodone.  Just seems that the environment for opioids is getting more hostile. If we were bigger, we d have a corporate initiative to combat this.

4.    The item above would also include additional step-edits, quantity limits, and more denials on PAs. I m hearing that but don t have a lot of specifics to back it up. I ll ask the DMs.

5.    I m hearing that reps feel  spread thin . I push back because I don t buy it. As Gavin said this morning, if you do the math on targets for each product and time invested, we should be able to sell four products. Where I will give some ground is that perhaps there is less time to protect the script as that sometimes requires a lot of legwork (and time).

6.    Can t ignore the obvious some reps have much better selling skills than others.

7.    Still hearing way too many discussions in which the starting dose is far too low. A setup to fail.

8.    Coming off of a good FY12, the decrease in bonus is a topic of discussion. That s where we come back with the money available through the contests.


Bill

Subject: FW: Follow up from AfBPM Summit Meeting (Nov 12-13)
From: "Webb, Kevin J" <kevin.webb@mallinckrodt.com>
Date: Fri, 11 Dec 2015 18:14:02 +0000
To: pdantonio@geron.org


Tricia,


FYI.  Message I sent to Debra Pasko at ASHP. 

 

I believe you had invited her based on your previous work experience.  Hopefully Debra will join our little band as we continue to drive access and patient safety forward.

Kevin

 

From: Webb, Kevin J
Sent: Friday, December 11, 2015 12:08 PM
To: 'dpasko@ashp.org'
Subject: Follow up from AfBPM Summit Meeting (Nov 12-13)



 

Debra,

 

On behalf of the Alliance for Balanced Pain Management (AfBPM), I would like to thank you for attending our recent Summit meeting held November 12-13 in Washington, DC.  Many of the points you raised during the work shop discussions were spot on regarding need to balance access to appropriate pain management with patient safety across the health care continuum, and the hospital/health system setting is of particular importance.

 

As you were leaving you had mentioned that the AfBPM would be a good fit with the ASHP.  The sole purpose of the AfBPM is to advance aligned coordination, singularity of message, and continuity in educating and empowering all stakeholders regarding responsible pain management. This includes the safe use, storage and disposal of pain medications.  The ASHP and the health-system pharmacist is crucial to this success, and we would be honored to have you as a member of the Alliance.

 

Attached is a brief slide deck that provides an overview, mission and structure of the Alliance for Balanced Pain Management.  After reviewing, let me know if you have any questions, or if would like to discuss in further detail.

 

For full disclosure I also wanted to make you aware that after the first of the year, management of the AfBPM will transition from Green Room Communications to a third-party, non-profit organization called the Alliance for Patient Access (AfPA).  This is a better long-term fit for the strategic direction and needs of the AfBPM, as the AfPA has the capabilities and capacity to guide the AfBPM to realize its full potential.  Over the next week I will be sending an announcement out the full membership, which I will copy you on, but I wanted to be completely transparent with you as you consider your decision.

 

Again, it was a pleasure meeting you, and look forward to your favorable reply.


Best regards,

Kevin

the renewal information to all valid account holders as their licenses come up for renewal and the respective business
obligingly complies with our request and forwards a copy of their current license, etc. In the case of the two
practitioner licenses we ve received in the past week or so, in both cases accounts were set up but we ve never sold

 Dr Marcin Chwistek provides expert commentary on FENTORA  (fentanyl buccal tablet) [CII] Dosing and Administration


  

 


 
 


 

 
 {Image 270x200}

 

 
 Featured Expert

  
 
 MARCIN CHWISTEK, MD, FAAHPM

Philadelphia, Pennsylvania


  
 

 


 
 


 

 This promotional program was developed and sponsored by Teva Pharmaceuticals, based on an interview with Marcin Chwistek, MD, FAAHPM.

Dr Chwistek received a fee for participation in this program.

  


 


 


 

 


 

   

 
 
 "I have found that FENTORA blister packs are highly portable and simple to open and discard. FENTORA makes it possible for patients to have the medication with them and permits buccal administration for either titration or maintenance dosing, and sublingual administration option for maintenance dosing. It is important to explain to patients that, in a pivotal trial, 70% of patients who found a successful dose of FENTORA during titration did so at a dose greater than or equal to 400 mcg."   Marcin Chwistek, MD, FAAHPM


FENTORA is indicated for the management of breakthrough pain in cancer patients 18 years of age and older who are already receiving and who are tolerant to around-the-clock opioid therapy for their underlying persistent cancer pain.

Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking around-the-clock medicine consisting of at least 60 mg of oral morphine daily, at least 25 mcg/hr of transdermal fentanyl, at least 30 mg of oral oxycodone daily, at least 8 mg of oral hydromorphone daily, at least 25 mg oral oxymorphone daily, or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid daily for a week or longer. Patients must remain on around-the-clock opioids while taking FENTORA.

This product must not be used in opioid non-tolerant patients because life-threatening hypoventilation and death could occur at any dose in patients not on a chronic regimen of opioids. For this reason, FENTORA is contraindicated in the management of acute or postoperative pain.

FENTORA is intended to be used only in the care of opioid-tolerant patients and only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable of and skilled in the use of Schedule II opioids to treat cancer pain.

Limitations of Use:
FENTORA may be dispensed only to patients enrolled in the TIRF REMS Access program.

Fatal respiratory depression has occurred in patients treated with FENTORA, including following use in opioid non-tolerant patients and improper dosing. The substitution of FENTORA for any other fentanyl product may result in fatal overdose.

Due to the risk of respiratory depression, FENTORA is contraindicated in the management of acute or postoperative pain including headache/migraine and in opioid non-tolerant patients.

  


 


 

 
 
 VIEW THE PROGRAM

 


  


 


 


 

 
 FENTORA Administration

Flexible and discreet administration options
Buccal administration for titration and maintenance dosing1
Sublingual administration for maintenance dosing1

FENTORA blister packets are highly portable and simple to open and discard
Once tablet is removed from blister unit, the tablet should be used immediately1
Patients should not split the tablet1
Instruct patients to leave tablet in place until it dissolves   generally 14 to 25 minutes1
After 30 minutes, if any tablet residue is left in mouth, patient may drink a glass of water to help swallow it1
The FENTORA tablet should not be crushed, chewed, or swallowed whole as this will result in lower plasma concentrations than when taken as directed1


  

 


 
 


 

 
IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION

WARNING: RISK OF RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, MEDICATION ERRORS,
ABUSE POTENTIAL

RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION
Fatal respiratory depression has occurred in patients treated with FENTORA, including following use in opioid non-tolerant patients and improper dosing. The substitution of FENTORA for any other fentanyl product may result in fatal overdose.

Due to the risk of respiratory depression, FENTORA is contraindicated in the management of acute or postoperative pain including headache/migraine and in opioid non-tolerant patients.

FENTORA must be kept out of reach of children.


The concomitant use of FENTORA with CYP3A4 inhibitors may result in an increase in fentanyl plasma concentrations, and may cause potentially fatal respiratory depression.

MEDICATION ERRORS
Substantial differences exist in the pharmacokinetic profile of FENTORA compared to other fentanyl products that result in clinically important differences in the extent of absorption of fentanyl that could result in fatal overdose.


When prescribing, do not convert patients on a mcg per mcg basis from any other fentanyl products to FENTORA.
When dispensing, do not substitute a FENTORA prescription for other fentanyl products.

ABUSE POTENTIAL
FENTORA contains fentanyl, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance, with an abuse liability similar to other opioid analgesics. FENTORA can be abused in a manner similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. This should be considered when prescribing or dispensing FENTORA in situations where the physician or pharmacist is concerned about an increased risk of misuse, abuse or diversion.

Because of the risk for misuse, abuse, addiction, and overdose, FENTORA is available only through a restricted program required by the Food and Drug Administration, called a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS). Under the Transmucosal Immediate Release Fentanyl (TIRF) REMS Access program, outpatients, healthcare professionals who prescribe to outpatients, pharmacies, and distributors must enroll in the program. Further information is available at www.TIRFREMSAccess.com or by calling 1-866-822-1483.

 


Contraindications:

FENTORA is contraindicated in opioid non-tolerant patients. Life-threatening respiratory depression and death can occur at any dose in opioid non-tolerant patients
FENTORA is contraindicated in the management of acute or postoperative pain including headache/migraine and dental pain
FENTORA is contraindicated in patients with known intolerance or hypersensitivity to any of its components or the drug fentanyl

Warnings and Precautions:

Clinically significant respiratory and CNS depression can occur. Monitor patients accordingly
FENTORA is not bioequivalent to other fentanyl products. Do not convert patients on a mcg per mcg basis from other fentanyl products
FENTORA contains a medicine in an amount which can be fatal to a child
Use with other CNS depressants and cytochrome P450 3A4 inhibitors may increase depressant effects including hypoventilation, hypotension, and profound sedation. Consider dosage adjustments if warranted
FENTORA may impair the ability to drive a car or perform other potentially dangerous tasks. Counsel patients accordingly
Titrate FENTORA cautiously in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or preexisting medical conditions predisposing them to respiratory depression and in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention
Application site reactions occurred in 10% of patients in clinical trials and ranged from paresthesia to ulceration and bleeding
Use FENTORA with caution in patients with bradyarrhythmias

Adverse Reactions:

Most common (frequency ?10%): nausea, dizziness, vomiting, fatigue, anemia, constipation, edema peripheral, asthenia, dehydration, and headache

Drug Interactions:

The concomitant use of FENTORA with CYP3A4 inhibitors may result in an increase in fentanyl plasma concentrations, and may cause potentially fatal respiratory depression
FENTORA is not recommended for use in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days, because severe and unpredictable potentiation by MAO inhibitors has been reported with opioid analgesics

Use in Specific Populations:

Administer FENTORA with caution to patients with severe hepatic or renal impairment

HDA to Testify before Senate HELP Committee on Drug Pricing

The Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) has called upon representatives from pharmaceutical supply chain organizations to testify at an October 17 hearing entitled, "The Cost of Prescription Drugs: How the Drug Delivery System Affects What Patients Pay, Part II." HDA Senior Vice President, Government Affairs and General Counsel, Liz Gallenagh, will testify on the role of distributors in the pharmaceutical supply chain. The hearing will take place at 10:00 a.m. in 430 Dirksen Senate Office Building. 

A full list of scheduled witnesses includes: 

Lori M. Reilly, Executive Vice President, Policy, Research & Membership, Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America, Washington, D.C. 
Chester "Chip" Davis, Jr., President and Chief Executive Officer, Association for Accessible Medicines, Washington, D.C.
Elizabeth A. Gallenagh, Senior Vice President Government Affairs and General Counsel, Healthcare Distribution Alliance, Arlington, Va. 
Mark Merritt, President and Chief Executive Officer, Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, Washington, D.C. 
Thomas E. Menighan, BSPharm, MBA, ScD(Hon.), FAPhA, Executive Director and Chief Executive Officer, American Pharmacists Association, Washington, D.C.

For more information, contact Jewelyn Cosgrove.

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}


One Month Remains to Register for the 2017 Blockchain Pre-Seminar Workshop and the Traceability Seminar

A short time remains to register for the November 8 Blockchain Pre-Seminar Workshop (hosted in partnership with IEEE) and HDA’s 2017 Traceability Seminar (November 8–10) in Washington, D.C. The pre-seminar workshop will provide attendees a look in to blockchain technology and how it can be applied to traceability in the pharmaceutical supply chain, while the Traceability Seminar will educate registrants on a variety of traceability topics and how they relate to DSCSA implementation efforts.

Register for the seminar and the workshop. For registration help or questions, contact HDA’s Meetings and Conferences at (703) 885-0278.  

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}

Congressional Hearings on the Opioid Crisis

Senate HELP Committee Discusses Federal Response to the Opioid Crisis

The Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee held a hearing last week (October 5) on "The Federal Response to the Opioid Crisis."  There were a range of questions about treatment, research, prescribing issues, concerns with illicit fentanyl and funding for addressing opioids, among others. It was noted that this is the first in a series of hearings on opioids. The next hearing will be in November (no date has been announced); the hearing will focus on state and local perspectives, exploring the challenges they face and the successes they have had in addressing the epidemic.

House Energy and Commerce Committee to Host Hearing on Opioids

The Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee is holding a "Member Day" tomorrow, Wednesday, October 11 at 10:15 a.m. to allow members both on and off the committee the opportunity to testify about the opioid epidemic.  

For more information, contact Jewelyn Cosgrove.

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}

Administration Names Acting DEA Administrator

Robert Patterson has been named Acting Administrator of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). Patterson is a career DEA Special Agent, having served with the agency since 1988. He had been serving, in effect, as Acting Deputy Administrator since late last year. An acting deputy administrator has not been named.

For more information, contact Ruth Miller.

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}

New Member Spotlight: Domino Amjet, Inc.

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}     HDA recently welcomed Domino Amjet, Inc. as a service provider member. Based in Gurnee, Ill., Domino has become the global solution provider for all product identification needs — including UDI and track and trace — for the most significant brands in the life science sector. Whether it’s serialized or variable printing, product marking or date coding, Domino Amjet and its products are a proven solution.

 

For more information, visit the company’s website or contact Paul Hammond, President.

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}

USP Announces Intent to Delay Chapter on Handling Hazardous Drugs

The United States Pharmacopeia (USP) has announced that it intends to delay the effective date of its General Chapter <800> Hazardous Drugs—Handling in Healthcare Settings until Dec. 1, 2019. The chapter, which relates to drugs identified by NIOSH as hazardous, describes standards that healthcare personnel, pharmacies, hospitals, physicians’ offices, and veterinarians should use to promote patient safety, worker safety, and environmental protection. Several states have discussed adopting the chapter into their requirements. The chapter does not impose requirements on wholesale distributors.

For more information, contact Ruth Miller.

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}

What’s Included in Your HDA Membership?

Make the most of your HDA membership by building close business relationships with wholesale distributor, manufacturers and service provider colleagues, while benefiting from their expertise with industry-created resources.

HDA’s website is full of information; you can search our online membership directory and access the service provider search, which gives you a list of HDA service provider members and the services they provide. Additionally, one of your many member benefits is access to HDA’s free educational publications, guidelines and forms.

Subject: The Hill Op-Ed: Elderly Risk and Opioids



 

Colleagues,

 

On Monday, July 13, 2015, the White House will host its official Conference on Aging, a once-a-decade summit that addresses policy strategy to meet the needs of America s elderly population.

 

We were successful in arranging to have the attached op-ed run in Friday s publication of The Hill, a key inside-the-beltway newspaper that is closely read by Members of Congress and Staff.  The op-ed draws attention to the health threats posed to the elderly by the use of opioids and calls for an alternative to opioids, such as intravenous acetaminophen.  The op-ed s call to action is for a broad discussion throughout the healthcare community on expanding options for treating pain in elderly patients, beginning with next week s White House Conference on Aging.

 

This is but one of several immediate steps we re taking to educate Members of Congress and Staff, as well as key patient groups, on alternatives to opioids, elevating the urgency of the issue so that it s top of mind in the context of the on-going national opioid debate.  We ll also be highlighting the op-ed to key congressional offices, including the two drug caucuses and the Senate Aging committee, and policy makers at the state level.

Kerlikowske to Leave ONDCP, Nominated as Commissioner of Customs and Border Protection

President Obama recently nominated the current director of the Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP), R. Gil Kerlikowske, as Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection. If he is confirmed by the Senate, President Obama will nominate a new director of the ONDCP, who will coordinate drug-control activities and related funding across the federal government.

For more information, contact Allison Tuszynski.
{top of page}

Reminder: DEA Hosting October Conference for Distributors

As reported in last week's Weekly Digest, the DEA is hosting a Distributor Conference on October 22 at the Gaylord National Resort and Convention Center in National Harbor, Md. Due to space limitations, this DEA-organized conference invites two representatives from each distributor registrant to attend on a first-come, first-served basis.

An agenda is not yet available, but DEA intends to address such topics as drug and chemical trends, Automation of Reports and Consolidated Orders System (ARCOS) reporting, record-keeping requirements, and "suspicious orders" reporting.

If you plan to attend, register directly with the DEA. Further information and directions for online registration can be found through their website, or by contacting DEA directly at ODLL@usdoj.gov.

For more information, contact Anita Ducca.
{top of page}

CMS Releases Responses to FAQ on the Open Payments Act and Holds Conference Call for Physicians

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) released responses to additional "Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)" last week. In response to FAQ 8980, CMS addresses the question of how distributors should report information in the "Product Indicator" data element. CMS stated that:

"Distributors that are considered applicable manufacturers because they hold title to a covered drug, device, biological or medical supply may report 'None' in the Product Indicator indicating that the payment or other transfer of value was not associated with any covered drugs, device, biological or medical supply if the payment or other transfer of value was related to the distributors full line of products, rather than any specific covered products."

Additionally, CMS hosted an August 8 conference call entitled, "Policy Updates on Payments and the Physician Resource Toolkit," which provided additional information for physicians on the Open Payments Act. View the PowerPoint presentation from the call; the audio recording and written transcript of the call will be posted here when available.

For more information, contact Kristen Freitas.
{top of page}

Distribution Center Challenge Update: AmerisourceBergen Hosts Alabama State Senator Jimmy Holley (R-31)


 
From Left: AmerisourceBergen's Dave Leverette, President, Oncology Supply, and Julie Eddy, Director, State Government Affairs; and State Senator Jimmy Holley (R-31). 

Alabama State Senator Jimmy Holley (R-31) visited AmerisourceBergen's Oncology Supply Center in Dothan, Ala., on July 18. AmerisourceBergen staff discussed a number of issues with the senator, including the challenges facing community oncology, Medicare reimbursement, compounding pharmacies and managed care systems. Senator Holley owns a compounding pharmacy with his son, who is a pharmacist in the community.

For more information on the Distribution Center Challenge, contact Jewelyn Cosgrove.

{top of page}

Learn Best Practices for Navigating Corporate Acquisitions and Divestitures at HDMA's Upcoming "Trade Management Seminar"

Geared toward individuals responsible for trade relations or account and vendor management, HDMA's "Trade Management Seminar" — September 23–24 at The Umstead Hotel in Cary, N.C. — will provide the opportunity to hear perspectives on building effective connections between distributors and manufacturers, solving key everyday problems and anticipating changes that may affect your company or one of your trading partners.

On Tuesday, September 24, Steve Noetzel, Director, Trade Accounts, Johnson & Johnson HealthCare Systems Inc.; and Dianne Pfahl, Vice President, Industry and Manufacturer Relations, Cardinal Health, Inc., will lead a session on, "The Angst of Acquisition." This session will present how product and corporate acquisitions or divestitures impact the supply chain, outline best practices for smooth transitions and but explore how to navigate these changes.

The full agenda is available through the HDMA website. For registration information, contact HDMA's Meetings & Conferences Department at (703) 885-0278.
{top of page}

FDA Withdraws OxyContin Approval

As noted in the April 23 Weekly Digest, FDA approved Purdue Pharma's reformulated OxyContin labeling changes and this week published a notice that the request for withdrawal of original formulation OxyContin was found to be not for reasons for safety and effectiveness. The FDA formally withdrew approval of original OxyContin; effective August 7, distribution of this product across states without an approved application is illegal.

For more information, contact Allison Tuszynski.

The Opioid Abuse Deterrence Act and DOJ Initiatives: Just What the Doctor Ordered?

Posted: 07 Dec 2017 08:48 PM PST

By John A. Gilbert & Larry K. Houck  

 For Americans under the age of 50, drug overdoses are now the leading cause of death.  DOJ, Attorney General Jeff Sessions Delivers Remarks Announcing New Tools to Combat the Opioid Crisis (Nov. 29, 2017) (here).   With evidence suggesting that nearly 80 percent of individuals addicted to heroin started out on opioid pain relievers, the link is clear that opioid prescriptions are driving this epidemic.   Rep. Mark Meadows, Opioid Abuse Deterrence, Research and Recovery Act (here).  These statements by government officials, one representing the Trump Administration, the other from Congress, provide a sobering picture of the nationwide opioid abuse epidemic and form the basis for two new actions designed to stem the opioid crisis.  On November 29, 2017, Congressman Mark Meadows (R-NC) introduced H.R. 4482, the Opioid Abuse Deterrence, Research, and Recovery Act of 2017.  On the same day, Attorney General Jeff Sessions announced several Department of Justice ( DOJ ) and Drug Enforcement Administration ( DEA ) efforts also aimed at addressing the crisis.

Opioid Abuse Deterrence, Research, and Recovery Act of 2017

The Opioid Abuse Deterrence, Research and Recovery Act ( the Act ) would amend the Federal Controlled Substances Act ( CSA ) to require DEA-registered and state-licensed practitioners authorized to prescribe schedule II or III controlled substances to submit a  certification  to DEA that they will not prescribe a schedule II or III opioid  for the initial treatment of acute pain  unless the prescribed quantity is for less than seven days or falls within a State-established prescription limit.  Acute pain  is defined as  pain with abrupt onset and caused by an injury or other process that is diagnostically determined to have minimal risk of escalating in intensity.    Acute pain  under the Act does not include chronic pain, pain treated as part of cancer care, hospice, end-of-life care, or palliative care.

Under the Act, the certification would not prevent practitioners from prescribing opioids approved by FDA for opioid use disorder treatment; for immediate, post-operative pain relief; or for longer than seven days if prescribing is consistent  with a clear medical standard of care,  provided that the practitioner documents the prescription in the patient s medical record and consults the State electronic health record system or prescription drug monitoring program.

The legislation would also require the FDA Commissioner to continue working with stakeholders and encouraging the development of abuse-deterrent opioids. In addition, to understand what led to the opioid crisis, the Act requires the Comptroller General to submit a report to Congress within two years on the health care policy changes that may have contributed to the increase in opioid overdoses and deaths.  The report must include:

A review of the federal health care-related legislative, administrative, and judicial decisions that affected access to pharmaceutical pain management strategies;
An analysis of the financial and non-financial costs and benefits of reversing or revising such decisions;
An analysis of the differences between State prescription drug monitoring programs;
 An analysis of the impacts of State and Federal prescribing limitations on patient medical outcomes; and
An analysis of the costs of using abuse-deterrent opioids compared to non-abuse-deterrent opioids.

Finally, the Act would require the FDA Commissioner to conduct a study on the feasibility of replacing the prescribing limits in the bill  with evidence-based clinical guidelines,  including a limitation  on the first opioid prescription for patients for an acute pain diagnosis  and  the incorporation into routine medical visits of evidence-based screening tools [to monitor] the misuse of opioids and other controlled substances. 

HPM Comments

We have long believed that effectively addressing the opioid epidemic requires focus on the physicians, doctors, dentists, and other practitioners who are the gatekeepers of public access to controlled substances. It is clear that overprescribing or inappropriate prescribing of controlled substances has been a significant cause in creating and sustaining the opioid abuse crisis.

The Act was clearly drafted with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention s ( CDC s ) Guidelines for Prescribing Opioids for Chronic Pain in mind. While the CDC guidelines voluntarily limit opioid prescribing for chronic pain, the Act limits only the first or initial prescription of schedule II or III opioids to treat acute pain to seven days unless the practitioner fulfills requirements to prescribe for a longer period.  In fact, the Act does not reference prescribing for chronic pain.  Both the Act and the CDC guidelines focus on a theme that we believe is a significant contributor to the opioid abuse problem, that is, overprescribing or inappropriate prescribing of controlled substances.  However, the mechanics of having a prescriber provide a  certification  to DEA is problematic.  There are no details on how prescribers would  certify  (e.g., during the application or renewal process).  More importantly, the Act does not address the regulatory effect of certifying or, even more significantly, failure to comply with the certification.  It also fails to address whether practitioners will self-certify or obtain certification for submission from an official or unofficial organization.  It is worth noting that the CSA and DEA regulations related to sales of pseudoephedrine, provide for a certification by retail sellers that they will not sell in amounts greater than allowed under the CSA.  21 U.S.C.   830(e)(1)(A)(vii); 21 C.F.R.    1314.35-.42, 1314.101-.103.  Regardless, the Act s requirements will make practitioners more carefully consider issuing a first opioid prescription for longer than seven days.  The inescapable downside is that some overly cautious practitioners may decline to issue necessary prescriptions to legitimate patients for longer than a week if they do not want to adhere to the requirements to do so or from fear that they will appear on DEA s radar.

We believe that mandatory training and education for practitioners is more critical and an alternative would be to require that all practitioners who intend to be registered with DEA to prescribe Schedule II controlled substances should certify that they have received such training.

DOJ and DEA Initiatives

Attorney General Sessions announced several initiatives including a restructuring of DEA Field Offices to focus on the opioid abuse problem. The Attorney General announced that DOJ was awarding $12 million to law enforcement agencies in states hit hard by illegal prescription opioid, heroin, and methamphetamine activity.  DOJ awarded $7 million through its Anti-Heroin Task Force Program to investigate heroin and illegal opioid distribution in states with high per capita levels of treatment admissions for heroin and other opioids, and $5 million through the Anti-Methamphetamine Program to states that have  demonstrated numerous seizures of precursor chemicals, finished methamphetamine, laboratories, and laboratory dump seizures.  DOJ, Attorney General Sessions and Acting DEA Administrator Patterson Announce New Tools to Address Opioid Crisis (Nov. 29, 2017) (here).

Attorney General Sessions also announced the formation of a new DEA Louisville Field Division. This new office will strengthen DEA investigation and enforcement efforts under a single Special Agent in Charge in Kentucky, Tennessee, and West Virginia.  The geographic area served by the new Louisville Field Division was previously distributed among the Detroit, Atlanta, and Washington, D.C., Field Divisions.  The Attorney General anticipates that consolidating Kentucky, Tennessee, and West Virginia within a single jurisdiction  will produce more effective investigations on heroin, fentanyl, and prescription opioid trafficking, all of which have a significant impact on the region.  Id.

Lastly, the Attorney General directed every U.S. Attorney to designate an Opioid Coordinator for their district by December 15th. The Attorney General s memo to all U.S. Attorneys instructed that Opioid Coordinators will be responsible for:

Facilitating intake of cases involving prescription opioids, heroin, and fentanyl;
Convening a task force of federal, state, local, and tribal law agencies to identify opioid cases for federal prosecution, facilitate interdiction efforts, and tailor their district s response to the needs of their communities;
Advising and training Assistant United States Attorneys on prosecuting opioid offenses;
Maintaining statistics on opioid prosecutions; and
Developing and evaluating the strategy to combat the opioid epidemic.

HPM Comments  

The creation of a new DEA Field Office focuses on several states particularly hard hit by the opiate abuse problem. Thus, it makes sense that DEA would consolidate resources to narrow the geographic scope to address these issues.  DEA drug investigations are better coordinated and more efficient when conducted within a single Field Division rather than multiple jurisdictions.  It also seems to us that the creation of an Opioid Coordinator should result in a more focused approach by U.S. Attorney offices to the opioid problem.  We note that in August 2017 the Attorney General had announced the formation of the Opioid Fraud and Abuse Detection Unit, which is a pilot program funding 12 prosecutors nationwide to focus on investigating and prosecuting health care fraud related to prescription opioids. Thus, DOJ/DEA is devoting significant resources to the fight against opioid abuse, which will likely result in more criminal, civil and administrative actions.

DEA Suspends Cardinal Health Distribution Facility: Cannot Sell Controlled Substances for Two Years

  

On May 15 the DEA announced a settlement agreement with Cardinal Health, a pharmaceutical wholesale distributor that suspends for two years its ability to sell controlled-substance medications from its Lakeland, Florida, distribution facility. In the agreement, Cardinal admits that its due diligence efforts for some pharmacy customers and its compliance with an earlier agreement signed in 2008 for similar violations at the same facility were, in certain respects, inadequate. The obligations of the agreement remain in full force and effect for a period of five years unless DEA agrees in writing to an earlier termination.The current settlement agreement also includes a signed Administrative Memorandum of Agreement whose terms apply to all Cardinal's 28 registered distribution facilities.

 

On February 3 of this year, DEA's Miami Field Division served an Immediate Suspension Order (ISO) against Cardinal Health's distribution center in Lakeland, Florida, alleging that this distribution center failed to maintain effective controls against the diversion of controlled substances, specifically oxycodone. It was not DEA's first action against Cardinal's Lakeland facility. In December 2007, DEA issued an ISO at the location as a result of its distribution of hydrocodone to 'rogue' internet pharmacies. That action, and similar actions at other Cardinal Health facilities across the United States, resulted in a $34 million fine.  Click here to read DEA's full press release.  

 

 

Information for Members on Electronic Prescribing of Controlled Substances   


Attached please find information forwarded by Surescripts related to electronic prescribing of controlled substances.  Given that it has been over two years since the DEA issued its interim final rule that allows the electronic prescribing of controlled substances, Surescripts is sharing the information here that lists those states in which prescribers reportedly are utilizing DEA-compliant systems.  

OIG Issues Report on Questionable Part D Billing 



 

 

The Office of Inspector General of the United States Department of Health and Human Services (OIG) recently issued a report on retail pharmacies with questionable Medicare Part D billing. Medicare Part D is a voluntary prescription drug benefit available to Medicare beneficiaries that went into effect on January 1, 2006. Since that time, the OIG and others have raised concerns about Part D billing. In several reports, OIG found that the program has limited safeguards in place and is vulnerable to fraud, waste, and abuse.

 

Moreover, recent cases have illustrated a variety of alleged fraud schemes by pharmacies. For example, one pharmacist who owned 26 pharmacies was charged with health care fraud and drug diversion. The pharmacist allegedly paid physicians to write prescriptions that were medically unnecessary and to direct patients to fill them at his pharmacies, which purportedly billed $37.7 million to Medicare.

 

In this report, OIG examined the Part D billing patterns of 59,000 retail pharmacies during 2009, which amounted to nearly 1 billion prescriptions. Through the study, investigators revealed contrasts between normal pharmacy practices and potential criminal behavior. Overall, the report found a pattern of questionable claims at 2,637 pharmacies around the country, including one pharmacy in Kansas that billed Medicare for more than 1,000 prescriptions for two patients in a single year. In total, Medicare paid $5.6 billion in possible fraudulent billings that year.  A copy of the report is found here.

BOSTON ?

A pair of pharmacies in Quincy and Norwood have been shut down by the

Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy following charges of
regulatory violations.
The pharmacies are co-owned by Dorchester resident Son Dinh and Christopher
Le of Stoughton.
The Quincy pharmacy, CarePro, had been granted a license to operate less
than eight months before it was officially suspended. The Norwood pharmacy,
Medi-Son, has had a license since the end of 2010.
Both Dinh and Le have been served with summary suspensions of their
pharmaceutical licenses. As Administrative Hearing Consul Beverly Cogut noted at
Dinh?s administrative hearing on Monday, summary suspensions are issued when
a ?continued threat to public health, safety or welfare? is believed to
have been found.
William Frisch, an investigator with the Office of Public Protection, said
at the hearing that he first visited CarePro in April, accompanied by his
partner and two agents from the federal Drug Enforcement Administration.
During the visit, Frisch said, he observed a number of violations of
pharmacy board regulations including a number of suspicious prescriptions for 30
mg tablets of the narcotic oxycodone for out-of-state patients. The
prescriptions, according to Frisch, originated from a pain center in Fort
Lauderdale, Fla.
Frisch also described deficiencies in the pharmacy?s record -keeping,
particularly regarding inventories and records of Schedule II drugs like
oxycodone. In one instance, Frisch said he found a vial of Ketamine that had come
from Medi-Son to fill a prescription without documentation that, according
to Dinh, had been misplaced.
Schedule II drugs include substances that the federal government holds to
have medical value, but have a high potential for abuse and addiction.
Although CarePro?s license to operate was not immediately suspended
following Frisch?s visit, the Norwood pharmacy, Medi-Son, was served with a
cease-and-desist order following a separate visit from the Office of Public
Protection investigators the previous day.
Then, during a follow-up visit to Medi-Son in May, investigators allegedly
found several prescriptions ? including one for Ritalin, also a Schedule II
drug ? that appeared to have been filled by CarePro.
Through his attorney, Dinh contends he had attempted to follow up the
investigator?s April visit with changes to his pharmacy?s policies, and was
simply the victim of opaque state pharmacy regulations.

Commercial colleagues,

I want to make you aware of a recent FDA request for an analysis of the available data (Clinical development and post marketing) for the incidence of allergic reactions (Anaphylaxis, Anaphylactoid, Urticaria, Angioedema, etc.) associated with Exalgo. They have indicated they believe this is attributable to an excipient, Sodium Metabisulfite (See agency letter of request below). This is an important request, and could have significant impact on Exalgo, up to and including labeling change or even reformulation. It is my understanding that sodium metabisulfite is a component of the HM active ingredient rather than the OROS technology (Phil, please correct if I am mistaken). We are working with the agency to identify the appropriate analysis methodology and when they agree, we will conduct the review of data and provide the requested information.

John,

Do we know the potential implication of a request for reformulation with a API source of HM that does not contain sodium metabisulfite? Has a measure of this nature been discussed with our manufacturing partner?

Thanks.

Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA) for EXALGO (hydromorphone HCl) 8-, 12-, and 16-mg
Extended-Release Tablets.
We also refer to your Periodic Safety Update Reports for Exalgo, received March 8 and June 30,
2011. These reports described cases of anaphylactic shock and pharyngeal edema/urticaria. A
preliminary search of the Adverse Events Reporting System (AERS) also identified cases
suggesting allergic reactions.
Given the occurrence of these cases, and the sodium metabisulfite component in the Exalgo
formulation, we request the following:
Review the Exalgo clinical development program, as well as your postmarket safety surveillance
system, to comprehensively describe cases of allergic reactions and hypersensitivity reactions

medical literature to identify any published cases.

section with narrative summaries for cases leading to discontinuation and a section with
narrative summaries for cases that qualified as serious adverse events. All cases should be
summarized in tabular form by preferred term, giving the number of cases and incidence
for each treatment arm. Please present data from randomized controlled trials separately
from open label trials.
* Describe separately the experience in the postmarket period. Each case should be
summarized in a narrative summary.

Police say nurse took meds from patients
By Julie Manganis and Ethan FormanStaff writersThe Salem NewsFri Jan 20, 2012,
05:00 AM EST
DANVERS — A now-former nurse at a Danvers assisted-living facility is facing
charges that she stole pain medications from at least six residents for months, secretly
replacing their Vicodin and oxycodone with a generic version of Tylenol.
Investigators were led to Amy Martin, 29, of 24 Barnard St., Marblehead, a registered
nurse, after a complaint in September from the niece of an elderly resident at
Brightview Danvers. She said the pills she found in her aunt's medication container did
not look like the ones she had been picking up for her at a pharmacy, according to a
police report.
Martin is due in Salem District Court this morning, where she is expected to be
arraigned on six counts of larceny of prescription drugs and a charge of possessing
Class B controlled substances — other patients' medications that police found after
they questioned her last October.
Martin confessed to police when confronted, according to court papers. When asked
what she thought as she deprived residents of their pain medications, she told
investigators she could not explain, other than to say that she herself was in pain
"every day."
The case came to light in September, when the niece went to officials at the assistedliving facility on Endicott Street.

MNKOI 0004228209

 She said that not only did the supposed Vicodin pills in her aunt's case look different,
but they had jagged edges where they had been split, according to Sgt. William
Carleton's report. The niece said she uses a pill splitter to cut her aunt's medications,
and that usually left smooth edges.
When officials at the facility checked the pills, they discovered that they were actually
acetaminophen.
The facility arranged to leave more Vicodin in the aunt's medications case, and within
a couple of days, those pills had been switched, as well.
The niece told officials that she had noticed something similar last January and had
asked Martin, the nurse working with her aunt, about it. Martin said she would look into
it, the niece said.
Management at Brightview contacted Danvers police at the beginning of October, and
over the next several weeks, an investigation — including hidden cameras placed in
several residents' rooms — revealed that more medication was being taken from
patients.
Martin was caught on camera taking the medication container of one patient to a
dining table, then returning it a few moments later. When investigators checked, the
prescription pills had been replaced with acetaminophen.
Martin, who had worked at the facility for about a year at that point, was questioned by
police on Oct. 25 and admitted to taking pills, Carleton wrote.
Police opted to seek a summons for her to appear in court instead of arresting her
immediately.
"They followed the best protocol to protect their residents," police Sgt. Robert
Bettencourt said of Brightview's role in the investigation. "They did the right thing and
followed the proper procedure to keep their residents safe."
"At Brightview Danvers, our residents' safety and well-being is our top priority," said
Beth Vellante, executive director of the facility, which has 185 residents.
"We applaud the alert action of our staff who immediately reported the former nurse's
inconsistency in standard procedure, and we appreciate the Danvers Police
Department for their guidance, support and direction throughout the investigation, as
well as their discretion and respect for our residents as the matter was investigated."

[RxNews] New Jersey doctor ran Oxycodone drug dealing scheme
ATT3714704.txt

Authorities say Montclair doctor ran
oxycodone drug-dealing scheme
Published: Thursday, March 24, 2011, 9:48 PM

Updated: Friday, March 25, 2011, 10:04 AM

By Jason Grant/The Star-Ledger
Follow

Share61
2
The doctor from Montclair trudged into the courtroom with the other handcuffed defendants in Newark federal court this
afternoon. Looking beat-tired, his face stricken with anxiety at times, he was arrested early in the morning and stood
accused of being the ringleader of 12 people who conspired to deal thousands of pills containing oxycodone — a
prescription-only drug that a prosecutor called the "new drug of choice" for New Jersey teenagers.
Federal authorities say the drug is a highly addictive analgesic — loaded with twice the potency of morphine — that's
used medically to treat chronic pain.
Michael Durante, a 56-year-old doctor of internal medicine who practices in Nutley, faces allegations that he regularly
wrote illegal pill prescriptions and pocketed thousands of dollars for it, all while conspiring with other defendants,
including several people who saw him as regular patients.
Looking disheveled in a wrinkled long-sleeve shirt, Durante listened as U.S. Magistrate Judge Michael Shipp ordered
that he could only be released into the custody of his brother, Mark, an oral surgeon, and only on a $1 million bond
secured by two homes he owns. Durante met the conditions.
The other defendants named in the complaint who appeared in court today were each released on $100,000 unsecured
bonds.
Prosecutor Anthony J. Mahajan's voice boomed across the courtroom as he argued the judge should hit Durante with a
high-amount, secured bond, and as he argued — successfully — that the court should bar Durante from practicing
medicine until the charge against him is resolved.
"There's a reason Dr. Durante is listed first on the complaint," Mahajan said. "He was at the top of the food chain and
was responsible for the chain reaction down the line."
He continued: "The oxycodone epidemic in New Jersey is the new drug of choice. Our kids here are taking it and
they're taking it in epidemic proportions. It can only come into the distribution channel in one way, and that's through
doctors like this."
When federal agents searched Durante's home today, they found a locked safe filled with hundreds of thousands of
dollars in cash, Mahajan added.
In the criminal complaint, federal authorities said Durante at one point wrote prescriptions for more than 1,000 pills in
just 10 days, and authorities alleged that some of his patients dealt the drug on the street for large profits.

Confidential

MAL-MI 000215771
MNKOI 0003438269

 The complaint also said one of the co-conspirators, Lawrence Gebo, a 62-year-old retired Newark police officer, was
plotting to get Durante a "gold" Fraternal Order of the Police card as a reward for writing the prescriptions. The cards
are normally reserved for the immediate family members of officers.
The conspiracy to distribute oxycodone started in January 2010, authorities alleged. If convicted on the charge, each of
the 12 defendants face up to 20 years in prison and a $1 million fine.

Mudri Associates Inc

Subject: Update: HENS MMA Webinar: August 15, 2016



 

Wanted to update you that response to the HENS webinar on minimizing opioid use has been very positive.

 

In addition, both ASRA (American Society for Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine) and the AAPM (The American Academy of Pain Medicine) are promoting the webinar on their respective meetings calendar.  See links:

Subject: HENS MMA Webinar: August 15, 2016



 

OFIRMEV Team,

 

Through the effort of the Collaborative for Effective Prescription Opioid Policies (CEPOP), they will host a webinar on Monday, August 15 which will highlight the work of the Michigan Health & Hospital Association Foundation and the Hospital & Healthcare Association of Pennsylvania and their efforts in minimizing opioid monotherapy and their work in advancing MMA.

 

As part of the CMS Partnership for Patients initiative, these two nationally prominent HENS have made great efforts in addressing opioid overuse in hospitals.  Michigan will take this opportunity to discuss their work utilizing the Michigan Opioid Safety Scale (MOSS) and Pennsylvania will highlight their Hospital and Practice Assessments.

 

The webinar will open with comments by Dr. Kate Goodrich, Director of the Center for Clinical Standards and Quality at CMS, and will conclude with comments from Dr. Anita Gupta, Vice Chair of Pain & Regional Medicine at Drexel University College of Medicine.  Rich Hamburg, Executive Director of Trust for America's Health and CEPOP co-founder will ?emcee the webinar.

 

As you can see, this will be an exciting program which will advance the MMA message, and encourage you to share this information with your accounts who may be interested in learning more about the work of these two HENs and their efforts in reducing opioid monotherapy.  Please be aware that the webinar will be limited to 500 participants, and spots are already filling up.  However, it will be also be available on demand following the live event on the 15th. 


Please let me know if you have any questions.


Thanks.

Kevin

We took fresh look at our model, and our sum-of-the-parts analysis for Acthar, the brand biz ex-Acthar, and the generics biz supports our $70 price target.

Our takeaway: Sum-of-the-parts analysis supports $70 per share
In this note we have built out separate income statements and DCFs for Acthar ($56 per share), Other Brands ex-Acthar ($61), and Specialty Generics ($11), which supports our belief that the stock at current levels remains attractive. The key overhang for the stock remains the sustainability of Acthar, particularly from potential competition, but our base case assumes significant competition already. In fact, without competition we believe that Acthar would be worth at least $100 per share. Given the stock currently trades at $46 and assuming our valuations for the other pieces of the company, this would imply that the market is attributing only $32 per share of value to Acthar. This valuation implies that Acthar sales would decline 16% CAGR from 2018-2025 as Acthar retains only 25% share with competition, which seems very extreme to us.

Additional thoughts
Some observers have pointed to different types of transactions, which potentially could unlock value, but at the end of the day, management may not move down any of these paths. It may instead just continue to add long-duration assets to the in-line portfolio and/or pipeline, which is really how it has added most value in the past. We would like to see diversification away from Acthar to help change the discussion versus a share buyback, which would probably help the stock in the short-term but not really change the discussion.

Thoughts on the stock: A favorable/risk reward
About a month ago during the week of the UBS Healthcare Conference the stock had moved below $40, and management talked about a sense of urgency and open-mindedness to think  out of the box  to get the stock higher. Since that time the stock has rebounded to $46, and this sense of urgency from management has somewhat resonated with investors. But nothing with respect to the company s fundamentals has changed, and most of the spec pharma sector is up over 10% as well, so we attribute much of the positive move to this sector performance and believe there is more to go on MNK.

Valuation: Maintaining our Buy and our price target of $70
Our PT is from sum-of-the-parts (vs prior EV/EBITDA) after absorbing $58 of net debt.

The use of intravenous acetaminophen for acute pain in the emergency department
 
Billy Sin, Mabel Wai, Tamara Tatunchak, Sergey M Motov
 
Academic Emergency Medicine: Official Journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine 2016 January 29
 
OBJECTIVES: Acetaminophen is a mainstay for pain management worldwide. The intravenous (IV) formulation has been widely used in Europe for more than 20 years in adults and children. In the United States, IV acetaminophen (APAP) obtained full approval from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2010. There is emerging literature to suggest the use of IV APAP for pain reduction in the Emergency Department (ED). This evidence-based review examines the evidence pertaining to the use of IV APAP for acute pain control in the ED.
 
METHODS: The MEDLINE and EMBASE databases were searched. Randomized controlled trials (RCT) that described or evaluated the use of IV APAP for acute pain in the ED were included. Duplicate articles, unpublished reports, abstracts, review articles, and non-English literature were excluded. The primary outcome of interest in this review was the difference in pain score between IV APAP and active comparator or placebo from baseline to a cutoff time specified in the original trials. Secondary outcome measures were the incidence of adverse events and reduction in the amount of adjuvant analgesics consumed by patients who received IV APAP. Methodological quality of the trials was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation criteria.
 
RESULTS: Fourteen randomized controlled trials (RCT) with various methodological flaws which enrolled a total of 1472 patients met the inclusion criteria. The level of evidence for the individual trials ranged from very low to moderate. In three of the fourteen trials, a significant reduction in pain scores was observed in patients who received IV APAP. The first trial found a significant reduction in mean pain scores when IV APAP was compared to IV morphine at 30 minutes after drug administration (4.7±2.3 vs. 2.9±2.2). In the second trial, patients who received IV APAP reported of lower pain scores (31.7mm+18, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 8.2-25.2) compared to those who received IV morphine (48.3mm+14.1, 95%CI: 8.2-25.2), 15 minutes after drug administration. A third trial found a significant reduction (p=0.005) in the mean pain scores when IV APAP was compared to intramuscular piroxicam at 90 minutes after drug administration. In the remaining 8 trials, pain scores were not statistically different when IV APAP was compared to other pain medications. The incidence of side effects associated with IV APAP was very low.
 
CONCLUSION: Fourteen randomized controlled trials with various methodological flaws provided limited evidence to support the use of IV APAP as the primary analgesic for acute pain control in patients who presents to the ED. This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.

Dear Lisa,

Please find attached the EXALGO Medication Guide with the FDA changes accepted. 

 

The only additional comment is to propose to add back under  Before taking EXALGO, tell your healthcare provider if you have a history of:  a bullet for  allergy to sulfites .  The rationale being that, although the chance of exposure to sulfites from the use of metabisulfite in the synthesis of the active ingredient, hydromorphone HCl, in EXALGO is minimal and acknowledging that metabisulfite is not an excipient used in the formulation of in EXALGO extended-release tablets, since  sulfite allergy  is included as a Contraindication and under Warnings and Precautions in the EXALGO PI and since patients are generally aware of an allergy to sulfites, it should be included in the Medication Guide.

 

As additional rationale, the following are excerpts from the CVS Pharmacy Health Information Center website article  Could You Be Allergic to Sulfites? . 

 

http://health.cvs.com/GetContent.aspx?token=f75979d3-9c7c-4b16-af56-3e122a3f19e3&chunkiid=644494

 

What Is Sulfite Sensitivity?


You are considered to be sensitive to sulfites if you have an allergic reaction after consuming or applying this preservative. The symptoms, which range from mild to severe, can include:

         Skin problems itchy skin, rash, hives

         Digestive problems stomach cramps, nausea, diarrhea

         Respiratory problems wheezing, cough, difficulty breathing, tightness in the chest

In extreme situations, a life-threatening allergic reaction called anaphylactic shock may occur, where the person is not able to breath and experiences a drop in blood pressure.

How common is this sensitivity? Actually, the FDA estimates that the number of Americans who are allergic to sulfites is low. But people with asthma seem to have a higher risk of experiencing a reaction to these chemicals.

 

Check Your Medication

Sulfites are added to many prescription and over-the-counter medications. Surprisingly, this preservative is often found in drugs used to treat asthma and allergies. Other types of medications that may have sulfites include:

         Drugs to treat vomiting and nausea

         Cardiovascular medicines

         Antibiotics

         Psychotropic drugs

         Medications delivered by IV

         Pain relievers

         Anesthetics

         Steroids and other medications to help with respiratory problems

Read the drug label carefully. If you have any questions, talk to your doctor and pharmacist.

 

Mallinckrodt is accepting of all the other FDA changes to the EXALGO Medication Guide.

Kind regards,

Linda
